lessons.title: 1.1 What is Mathematics?

activities.prompt: What might mathematics reveal in the world around you?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Pattern Tour
activities.body:
Your journey starts at home, where patterns wait in familiar objects. You see them at school and in the movements of the sun, moon and stars.

Next, you go shopping and watch patterns appear. In a kitchen, cooking follows patterns too. You recognise them while throwing a ball or playing games.

You can find patterns in nature and all around you. Outside, changing weather shows another pattern. Technology shows patterns as well. Mathematics gives you a way to search for them and explore why they exist.

Now your curiosity becomes the tool. You look for patterns and ask for explanations. This search can be fun and creative.

Mathematicians think of mathematics as both an art and a science. An explanation can travel far beyond where you discovered it. Mathematical discoveries can help humanity move forward.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Patterns Are Everywhere
activities.body: Mathematics is mostly about finding patterns. It also asks why patterns exist. You can see patterns in nature, homes and schools. You can see patterns in shopping, cooking, games, weather and technology. Finding patterns and explaining them can be fun and creative. Mathematicians see mathematics as both an art and a science.
keyPoints: Mathematics looks for patterns.
It explains why patterns exist.
Patterns appear all around us.
activities.explanation: Look closely: patterns and their explanations are everywhere.

lessons.title: 1.2 Patterns in Numbers

activities.prompt: Can you spot the hidden rule inside a line of numbers?

activities.title: Patterns in Numbers
activities.body:
You begin with a simple idea. Patterns of numbers are among the most basic patterns in mathematics. The counting numbers begin with 0 and continue in order. Number sequences are a basic and fascinating kind of mathematical pattern. Number theory studies patterns in whole numbers.

Now you meet two clear sequences. The odd-number sequence begins 1, 3, 5, 7 and continues with larger odd numbers. The even-number sequence begins 2, 4, 6, 8 and continues with larger even numbers.

Next, you discover growing number patterns. The triangular-number sequence begins 1, 3, 6, 10 and 15. The square-number sequence begins 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25. The cube-number sequence begins 1, 8, 27, 64 and 125.

Finally, you follow other sequences. The Virahānka-number sequence begins 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and 13. The powers-of-2 sequence begins 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. The powers-of-3 sequence begins 1, 3, 9, 27 and 81. You now see many patterns, and number theory helps you study them.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

lessons.title: 1.3 Visualising Number Sequences

activities.prompt: How can pictures reveal the hidden patterns in number sequences?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Seeing Number Sequences
activities.body:
Imagine meeting a number sequence. You wonder how its pattern grows. Pictures can make the pattern easier to see. You can use them to explore relationships. You can inspect the pattern and its relationships.

Table 1 gives you picture-based examples. The first seven sequences in Table 1 are represented with pictures. Each picture offers a visual clue about the pattern. Looking closely helps you understand the mathematical pattern.

Now look at 36 dots. You can arrange them to make a triangle. You can also arrange them to make a square. The number 36 is therefore both triangular and square.

Next, meet the sequence 1, 7, 19 and 37. This sequence is called hexagonal numbers. The pictures help you understand the sequence and its relationships.

Finally, pictures offer a pictorial way to think about powers of 2. They help you understand number sequences and their relationships. The same number can be shown in different ways. Each way can play a different role. Perhaps you will now see why pictures are so useful.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Seeing Number Sequences

Thirty-six dots can form both a triangle and a square. The same number can be shown in different ways and play different roles. The sequence 1, 7, 19 and 37 is called hexagonal numbers. Powers of 2 can also be thought about using a picture.
keyPoints: Pictures can show many number sequences.
Diagrams help us understand patterns.
The same number can have different roles.

activities.title: Patterns into Squares
activities.body:
You begin with counting dots because a picture can help explain a mathematical pattern. Arrange the dots in square grids. Each grid lets you see how square numbers can be made.

Now add odd numbers one after another. The pattern of adding odd numbers continues forever. A picture can show what the growing pattern looks like.

When you add the first six odd numbers, the sum becomes clear in a picture. The dots can form a square grid. You can count them and recognise a square number.

Try another route. Add counting numbers up and then down. The total gives a square number. This gives you another way to reach a square number.

You have seen that adding odd numbers gives square numbers. Pictures make these patterns easier to understand. You can explore the pattern yourself, as it continues forever.

activities.title: A Tour of Shape Patterns
activities.body:
Come with me on a shape-pattern tour. You discover that patterns of shapes are important and basic patterns in mathematics. You will also explore dimensions and geometry. Geometry is the branch that studies patterns in shapes.

You begin with shapes that may have one, two or three dimensions. Then you meet shapes with even more dimensions. As you move through the table, each example invites a closer look.

Next, you meet shape sequences. These are an important kind of shape pattern. The polygon examples in the table run from the triangle through to the decagon. You follow their place in the table.

Your tour also includes regular polygons and complete graphs from K2 to K6. The shape sequences include these examples too. You see both kinds included among the shape sequences.

At the end, you find more patterns in the same table. It includes stacked squares, stacked triangles and the Koch snowflake. You finish your tour with several different pattern examples. This collection shows why patterns of shapes matter in mathematics.

lessons.title: 1.6 Relation to Number Sequences

activities.title: Shapes and Numbers
activities.body:
Imagine you begin a journey through a world where shapes become clues. You discover surprising relationships between shape sequences and number sequences. These relationships help you study both kinds of sequence.

The sides of these regular polygons follow the counting numbers starting at 3. You meet the triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon and other named shapes along the way.

Now look closely at every regular polygon. You see equal-length sides and equal angles. You can compare these features as your journey continues.

When you trace a closed figure, you find another clear rule. The number of sides equals the number of corners, helping you connect shape and number.

Next, your tour reaches the Koch snowflake. You watch its first three shapes have 3, 12 and 48 line segments. You see a sequence unfold before your eyes.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Links between shapes and numbers
activities.body: Shape sequences and number sequences can be related in surprising ways. The sides of regular polygons follow counting numbers starting at 3. A regular polygon has equal-length sides and equal angles. In any closed figure, the number of sides equals the number of corners. The Koch snowflake forms a shape sequence. Its first three shapes have 3, 12 and 48 line segments.
keyPoints: Regular polygon sides follow counting numbers starting at 3.
Regular polygons have equal-length sides and equal angles.
Closed figures have equal numbers of sides and corners.
activities.explanation: These links help you compare shape sequences with number sequences.

activities.title: A Tour of Shapes
activities.body:
Imagine you arrive at a mark showing one exact place. You call this a point. You cannot give this point length, breadth or height. You name it with one capital letter, such as A. You say its name before its letter.

Now picture two points joined by the shortest path. You have a line segment, with two end points. You can write it as AB or BA. You can extend it beyond both of its end points.

Now step back from the segment. You meet a line, which has no end. Your line continues in both directions. You find that two points determine only one line.

Now choose a starting point. You draw a ray from there. The point where it starts is its initial point. You name the ray using its starting point and another point on it.

Tour complete: points mark places, segments join them, lines continue, and rays begin.

activities.prompt: How can you tell how much an angle has turned?

activities.title: An Angle Tour
activities.body:
You meet two rays with a common starting point. Together, they form an angle. The starting point is the vertex. You may see a small curve marking the angle there. The symbol ∠ can replace the word angle.

You can name this angle using only its vertex. You can also name it Angle DBE or Angle EBD. The vertex must always be the middle letter. In both names, B stays in the middle.

Now picture a pair of scissors. Opening its blades forms an angle. You open them wider, and more turning happens. You close them slightly, and less turning happens.

Next, imagine a compass. Turning its arms forms an angle. The amount of rotation decides the angle’s size. More turning makes a greater angle. Less turning makes a smaller angle. Your tour ends with two rays, one vertex, and a new way to see turning.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

Compass arms and scissor blades can form angles.

lessons.title: Comparing Angles and Making Rotating Arms

activities.prompt: How can you prove that two angles are equal?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Comparing Angles and Making Rotating Arms
activities.body:
You meet two hinged jaws, ready to compare their openings. A wider opening of the jaws makes a larger angle. You can test this by opening them differently.

Now you place one angle over the other. The vertices must overlap when two angles are superimposed. Superimposition helps you see which angle is smaller or larger.

If their matching corners and arms overlap, the angles are equal. Equal angles also need equal amounts of rotation. Two angles are equal when their matching rays lie exactly on each other.

Next, you move a transparent circle over a figure. The centre of the circle must be on the angle’s vertex. You mark where the arms pass through the circle.

Finally, you make rotating arms with two straws and a paper clip. You fit them into a slit. The arms fit when their angle equals the slit angle.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Compare angles and make rotating arms
activities.body: An angle can be compared by placing one over the other. This is called superimposition. The vertices are corners, and they must overlap. You can see which angle is smaller or larger. Equal angles have matching corners and overlapping arms. They need equal amounts of rotation. A transparent circle helps compare angles. Its centre must be on the angle’s vertex. Make rotating arms using two straws and a paper clip.
keyPoints: Placing one angle over another is superimposition.
Overlapping vertices help us compare smaller and larger angles.
Equal angles need matching arms and equal amounts of rotation.
activities.explanation: First superimpose the angles. Then check their corners and arms.

activities.title: A Tour of Special Angles
activities.body:
Imagine a folded sheet opening before you. Its two arms rest in a straight line. Together, they form a straight angle. A ray can divide this angle into two smaller angles.

Now fold the sheet so the arms meet at right angles. The equal angles made by folding are called right angles. Each right angle looks like the letter L. Lines meeting at right angles are called perpendicular lines. One straight angle contains two right angles. So a right angle is exactly half of a straight angle.

Some angles are less wide than a right angle. These smaller angles are called acute angles. Acute means sharp. Other angles open wider than a right angle. However, each one stays smaller than a straight angle. These are called obtuse angles. Obtuse means blunt.

Can you spot two lines meeting at right angles? Try drawing one straight angle and then splitting it with a ray. The two parts will be smaller angles. Then compare them with right, acute, and obtuse angles. Angles are classified into three groups.

Acute means sharp, and obtuse means blunt. Angles have three groups.

Acute means sharp, while obtuse means blunt.

activities.title: Measuring Angles
activities.body:
Imagine you meet a full circle. It is divided into 360 equal parts. Each part has an angle measure of one degree. An angle's measure is the number of one-degree parts inside it. A full turn measures 360 degrees.

Now you meet a straight angle. It measures 180 degrees. Then you find a right angle. That measures 90 degrees.

Your next tool is a protractor. This tool measures angles. Place its centre on the angle's vertex. Make one arm pass through the zero mark. Let the other arm turn through the required number of degrees. Then you can read the angle's measure.

Finally, you look for the middle of an angle. Getting half of an angle is called bisecting the angle. The line that bisects it is its angle bisector. You can now measure angles and split them carefully.

A protractor measures angles. Put its centre on the angle’s vertex. One arm must pass through the zero mark. The other arm must turn through the required degrees. Bisecting means getting half of an angle.
keyPoints: A full circle has 360 one-degree parts.
A protractor measures angles in degrees.
Bisecting an angle means getting half of it.

activities.title: A Tour of Angles
activities.body:
Imagine you are visiting a family of angles. Each one has a size, and you can measure these sizes in degrees.

During your tour, you meet several kinds of angles. You compare their sizes using degrees.

First, you meet the right angle. It measures 90°. Next, an acute angle appears. This angle is smaller than a right angle. So, it is smaller than 90° too.

Then you reach an obtuse angle. It is greater than a right angle and less than a straight angle. In degrees, it is greater than 90° and less than 180°. A straight angle comes next. It measures 180°. You now have useful angle sizes to compare.

Your journey continues to a reflex angle. It is greater than a straight angle. Its size is greater than 180° and less than 360°. You finish by comparing every angle you have met.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Meet the angle types
activities.body: An angle can be measured in degrees. A right angle measures 90°. A straight angle measures 180°. An acute angle is smaller than a right angle. An obtuse angle is greater than a right angle and less than a straight angle. A reflex angle is greater than a straight angle. It is greater than 180° and less than 360°.
keyPoints: A right angle measures 90°.
An obtuse angle is between a right angle and a straight angle.
A reflex angle is greater than 180° and less than 360°.

It then turns farther, past 180° but before 360°.
That turn is a reflex angle because it is greater than 180° and less than 360°.
So the first turn is a right angle, while the later turn is a reflex angle.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Numbers and Taller Neighbours

activities.prompt: What number might belong to each child in a line?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Taller Neighbours
activities.body:
You meet children standing in a line, and each child has a number to say. Numbers help us organise our lives in many different ways. We use numbers to count things. Your number counts taller neighbours beside you. It tells how many taller neighbours you have.

For each child, begin with their neighbours. If only one neighbouring child is taller, you say 1. If both neighbouring children are taller, you say 2. If neither neighbouring child is taller, you say 0. Each child’s number tells how many taller neighbours the child has.

At the ends, you check the rule. Children at the ends of a line cannot say 2. Their number still counts the taller neighbours they have.

Now imagine five children standing from shortest to tallest. Four children can say 1 and the last can say 0. You look from one child to the next. You count the taller neighbours and check each answer.

Try another arrangement of five children. At most two children can say 2. You can count taller neighbours and use 0, 1, or 2.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Counting Taller Neighbours
activities.body: Numbers help us organise lives. Each child says a number showing how many neighbours are taller. It is 1 when only one neighbour is taller. It is 2 when both neighbours are taller. It is 0 when neither neighbour is taller. Children at the ends of a line cannot say 2. Children of the same height can all say 0. In five children, at most two can say 2.
keyPoints: Each number shows how many neighbours are taller.
The numbers 0, 1, and 2 show the taller-neighbour count.
Children at the ends cannot say 2.
activities.explanation: These numbers help us compare the heights of neighbouring children.

activities.prompt: Five children stand in a line from shortest to tallest. What does each child say, and why?
steps: In this order, every child except the last has one taller neighbour.
The last child says 0 because its only neighbour is shorter.
The first four children say 1 because each has one taller neighbour.
So four children say 1 and the last child says 0.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.title: One Taller Neighbour
activities.prompt: A child has two neighbours. One neighbour is taller than the child. The other is not. How many taller neighbours does the child have?
activities.explanation: Only one neighbour is taller. So the answer is 1.

activities.title: No Taller Neighbours
activities.prompt: A child says ______ when neither neighbouring child is taller.
activities.hint: Think of the number used for no taller neighbours.
activities.explanation: Neither neighbour is taller, so the child's number is 0.

activities.title: Match the Neighbours
activities.prompt: Match each description with the child's number.
activities.explanation: Each number tells how many neighbouring children are taller.

activities.title: Children of the Same Height
activities.prompt: What can all children say when they have the same height?
activities.explanation: No child is taller than another child of the same height.

activities.title: Order the Numbers
activities.prompt: Put the child numbers in order from fewer taller neighbours to more.
activities.explanation: The order is 0, 1, then 2 because the taller-neighbour counts grow.

activities.prompt: Five children stand in a line. A child at an end says that two neighbours are taller. Why is this claim wrong?
options: An end child has only one neighbour.
The taller children are both neighbours.
The end child has two taller neighbours.
Two children in this line can say 2.

It treats nearby taller children as neighbouring children.
It forgets that an end child has only one neighbour.
It answers about other children instead of the end child.

activities.explanation: An end child has only one neighbour, so cannot say 2.

activities.prompt: At a playground, five children stand from tallest to shortest. The tallest stands first. What numbers can they say?
options: The first says 0; four others say 1.
The first says 1; four others say 0.
The first says 2; four others say 1.
The first says 0; four others say 2.

It wrongly treats the tallest child as having a taller neighbour.
An end child has only one neighbour, so cannot say 2.
The other four each have one taller neighbour, not two.

activities.explanation: Only the first has no taller neighbour; the other four have one.

activities.prompt: Five children wait in a queue. A middle child has two taller neighbours. An end child has one taller neighbour. Which child can say 2?
options: The middle child can say 2; the end child says 1.
The end child can say 2; the middle child says 1.
Both children can say 2 because each has a taller neighbour.
Both children can say 1 because each has one taller neighbour.

why.The end child can say 2; the middle chil: It ignores that only the middle child has two taller neighbours.
why.Both children can say 2 because each has: It counts one taller neighbour as enough for every child.
why.Both children can say 1 because each has: It treats one taller neighbour as the same number as two.

activities.explanation: The middle child has two taller neighbours; the end child has one.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Finding Supercells

activities.prompt: What might make one table cell a special discovery?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Supercell Hunt
activities.body:
You begin a quiet hunt for special cells in a table. A supercell holds a number larger than its adjacent cells. Neighbouring cells sit immediately to the left, right, top and bottom.

First, you compare 626 with 577 and 345. It is a supercell because 626 is larger than both neighbours. Next, 200 is not a supercell, because it is smaller than 577. Then 198 wins, because its only adjacent cell contains 109.

The largest number in a table is always a supercell. You look for the biggest value first. The smallest number can never be one. You wonder whether every table must contain a supercell. The answer is no. It is impossible to fill a table with different numbers and have no supercells.

You then complete Table 2 using the digits 1, 0, 6, 3 and 9. Its largest number is 96,310, which is always a supercell. Finally, you swap the digits 1 and 6 in 62,871. This creates four supercells, giving your hunt a surprising end.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What is a Supercell?
activities.body: A supercell holds a number larger than every adjacent cell. Adjacent cells sit immediately to the left, right, top and bottom. For example, 626 is a supercell because it is larger than 577 and 345. This rule helps you spot special cells in a number table.
keyPoints: A supercell is larger than every adjacent cell.
Adjacent cells are immediately left, right, top and bottom.
626 is larger than 577 and 345.
activities.explanation: Compare a cell with the numbers beside it to find a supercell.

activities.prompt: A cell holds 200. Its neighbour holds 577. Is 200 a supercell?
steps: First, check the number in the adjacent cell.
The adjacent cell holds 577, which is larger than 200.
Since 200 is smaller than its neighbour, 200 is not a supercell.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.title: Supercells in a Table
activities.body: In any finished table, the largest number is always a supercell. The smallest number can never be one. If every cell held a different number, at least one supercell would still exist. These rules help you check tables without examining every cell.
keyPoints: The largest number in a table is always a supercell.
The smallest number can never be a supercell.
A table with different numbers must contain a supercell.
activities.explanation: A table with different numbers must contain at least one supercell.

activities.title: Spot the Supercell
activities.prompt: 626 is a supercell because it is larger than 577 and 345.
activities.explanation: 626 is larger than both 577 and 345, so it is a supercell.

activities.title: Choose the Correct Statement
activities.prompt: Which statement about 200 is correct?
options: It is not a supercell.
It is larger than 577.
It is larger than 345.
It is the largest number in a table.
activities.explanation: 200 is smaller than 577, so it is not a supercell.

activities.title: Find the Neighbour
activities.prompt: Neighbour cells are right next to a cell, on its ______, right, top and bottom.
activities.hint: Think of the sides of a square.
activities.explanation: Left is one direction a neighbour cell can be in.

activities.prompt: What does the comparison between 198 and 109 show?
options: 109 is larger than 198.
198 equals 109.
198 is a supercell.
198 is smaller than 109.
activities.explanation: 198 is larger than its only adjacent cell, 109, so it is a supercell.

activities.title: Match Each Number
activities.prompt: Match each number with its correct comparison.
activities.explanation: 626 and 198 are larger than their adjacent numbers. 200 is smaller than 577.

activities.title: Order the Numbers
activities.prompt: Put these numbers in order from smallest to largest.
activities.explanation: The order is 626, 62,871, then 96,310.

activities.title: After Swapping Digits
activities.prompt: How many supercells are created after swapping 1 and 6 in 62,871?
activities.explanation: Swapping 1 and 6 in 62,871 creates four supercells.

activities.prompt: A row of three cells contains 6, 10, and 2 points, with 6 greater than 2 and 10 larger than both. How many more points is the middle supercell than its larger neighbour?
activities.explanation: The middle cell contains 10 points, and its neighbours contain 6 and 2 points. The middle cell is the supercell, and 6 is its larger neighbour. Subtract the larger neighbour: 10 - 6 = 4 points.
steps: The middle cell contains 10 points, and its neighbours contain 6 and 2 points.
The middle cell is the supercell, and 6 is its larger neighbour.
Subtract the larger neighbour: 10 - 6 = 4 points.
activities.hint: Find the larger of the two cells next to the middle cell.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Number Lines and Digit Sums

activities.prompt: Can you discover why some different numbers have matching digit sums?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Number Line and Digit Sums
activities.body:
You begin with a number line, where numbers can be placed in their correct positions. The activity gives you eleven numbers to place. Start writing from 1, 2, 3 and continue onwards. As you work, you can check each number’s position.

You begin writing numbers from 1, 2, 3 and continue onwards. Along the way, you notice nine one-digit numbers. Next, you meet a digit sum. A digit sum is found by adding up the digits of a number.

Now you compare 68, 176 and 545. Their digit sums are the same. Add the digits in each number, and you can see this pattern. You might wonder what connects these separate numbers.

Then you explore consecutive three-digit examples. Their digit sums are multiples of 3. You can try each example and find its digit sum. You can use the number line to place your examples.

Some numbers with digit sum 14 are 248, 653, 356, 815 and 833. You can make numbers with digit sum 14 increasingly large. By placing numbers and adding their digits, you discover more about number patterns.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Number Lines and Digit Sums
activities.body: Number lines place numbers in correct positions. One activity gives eleven numbers to place. Counting starts at 1 and continues onwards. Nine numbers have one digit. A digit sum comes from adding digits. 68, 176 and 545 share a digit sum. Consecutive three-digit examples have digit sums that are multiples of 3. Numbers with digit sum 14 include 248, 653, 356, 815 and 833. Such numbers can become increasingly large.
keyPoints: Numbers have correct positions on a number line.
Counting starts at 1 and continues onwards.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Number Patterns, Collatz and Games

activities.prompt: What might happen when you keep following a number’s special rule?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Following Numbers
activities.body:
You begin with a number pattern. One row has eight 32s, so your eyes search for order. Numbers can reveal patterns and give information, even when you are not sure what to expect.

Now you meet Collatz. For an even number, you divide it by two. For an odd number, you multiply it by three and add one. These steps turn a starting number into a sequence.

You try four sample sequences and watch each one. Each eventually reaches 1. Collatz conjectured that every sequence will reach 1. However, it is still unknown whether his conjecture is true.

Next, estimation helps. You do not need an exact count when an estimate is enough. Paromita estimated that her class had about 100 children. Her estimate gives useful information without an exact count.

Then come two number games. In the first, players add 1, 2 or 3 to the previous number. In the second, they add numbers from 1 to 10. Numbers support puzzles and games, and these orderly steps are computational thinking.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Numbers Help Us
activities.body: Number patterns help us spot order. One pattern has a row containing eight 32s. Collatz rules divide even numbers by two. Odd numbers are multiplied by 3, then 1 is added. All four samples reach 1, but it remains unknown whether every sequence will. Estimates help when exact counts are unnecessary. Numbers support games. Orderly steps for using numbers are called computational thinking.
keyPoints: Even numbers are divided by two in Collatz sequences.
Odd numbers are multiplied by 3, then 1 is added.
Collatz's conjecture is still unknown.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect number patterns, Collatz, estimation, games and computational thinking.

Treat the samples as support, not proof for every sequence.

activities.prompt: A Collatz sequence can contain 32 and 3. Which rule correctly gives the next step?
options: Divide 32 by two; multiply 3 by three and add one.

Divide 32 by two; multiply 3 by two and add one.
Add three to 32; multiply 3 by three and add one.

why.Multiply 32 by two; multiply 3 by three: This wrongly multiplies the even number 32 instead of dividing it.
why.Divide 32 by two; multiply 3 by two and: This wrongly divides the odd number 3 instead of multiplying it.
why.Add three to 32; multiply 3 by three and: This wrongly adds to the even number 32 instead of dividing it.

activities.explanation: It applies division to even 32 and the odd rule to 3.

activities.prompt: Four Collatz samples reach 1. A child says this proves the conjecture. What is the best reply?
options: Samples support it, but whether every sequence reaches 1 remains unknown.
The samples prove that every possible Collatz sequence will reach 1.
The samples show that other Collatz sequences can never reach 1.
The samples show that Collatz never conjectured that sequences reach 1.

why.The samples prove that every possible Co: Four samples cannot prove a claim about every possible sequence.
why.The samples show that other Collatz sequ: This wrongly says other sequences cannot reach 1, although samples do.
why.The samples show that Collatz never conj: This wrongly denies the conjecture Collatz actually made.

activities.explanation: The samples support the idea, but the full conjecture remains unknown.

activities.prompt: Paromita says her class has about 100 children. A friend says this means exactly 100 children. What is the mistake?
options: An estimate gives a rough count, not an exact count.
The number 100 must be exact because it was estimated.
About 100 children cannot describe the size of a class.
Only number patterns can give information about a class size.

why.The number 100 must be exact because it: This wrongly treats an estimate as an exact count.
why.About 100 children cannot describe the s: The estimate does give a useful idea of the class size.
why.Only number patterns can give informatio: Numbers can support estimation even without an exact count.

activities.explanation: An estimate is enough when an exact count is not needed.

activities.prompt: In the first game, players add 1, 2 or 3. One player adds 10 to the previous number. Why is that move not allowed?

The first game only allows multiplying by 3 and adding 1.
The first game allows adding any number, including 10.

why.The first game only allows adding number: That rule belongs to the second game, not the first.
why.The first game only allows multiplying b: The odd Collatz rule does not control the first game.
why.The first game allows adding any number,: The first game has a limit, so adding 10 is outside it.

activities.explanation: The first game limits each move to adding 1, 2, or 3.

activities.prompt: A child plans moves for a number game. Which plan shows computational thinking?
options: Choose a move, add 1, 2, or 3, then check the total.
Pick any number, change it often, and never explain the choices.
Draw eight 32s in a row without using any rule.
Use one Collatz step for both even and odd numbers.

why.Pick any number, change it often, and ne: Changing numbers without a plan does not show orderly steps.
why.Draw eight 32s in a row without using an: The row has no orderly steps for using the numbers.
why.Use one Collatz step for both even and o: This wrongly says even and odd numbers use the same step.

activities.explanation: It uses clear, orderly steps to work with numbers.

activities.prompt: Signs show prices, and puzzles give number clues. Which pair shows numbers doing useful work?

A price sign hides information, and a number puzzle stops all play.
A price sign needs Collatz steps, and a number puzzle needs odd steps.
A price sign counts eight 32s, and a number puzzle estimates children.

why.A price sign hides information, and a nu: Signs inform people, while number puzzles support play rather than stop it.
why.A price sign needs Collatz steps, and a: Collatz is separate from the number uses in shops and puzzles.
why.A price sign counts eight 32s, and a num: This wrongly mixes a pattern count and an estimate with other uses.

activities.explanation: Numbers convey information and can support puzzles and games.

activities.context: Five children stand in a line, ordered from shortest to tallest. Each child says a number showing how many neighbouring children are taller. The four children before the tallest each have one taller neighbour, while the tallest has none. activities.prompt: Before the swap, why do four children say 1 while the tallest child says 0?
options: One adjacent child is taller for each child except the tallest, who has none.
Every child has exactly one taller child somewhere in the line.
Each of the four shorter children has two taller neighbours.
The tallest child is treated as 1 because it has a neighbour.

why.Every child has exactly one taller child: A child counts only taller neighbours, not taller children anywhere in the line.
why.Each of the four shorter children has tw: The shorter children do not each have taller children on both sides.
why.The tallest child is treated as 1 becaus: The number shows how many neighbours are taller, so the tallest child says 0.

activities.explanation: Each of the first four children has one taller neighbour, while the tallest has no taller neighbour.

activities.context: Five children stand in a line, ordered from shortest to tallest. Each child says a number showing how many neighbouring children are taller. The four children before the tallest each have one taller neighbour, while the tallest has none. If the shortest and tallest children swap places, the children still remain in the same line, and everyone must use the new neighbours.
activities.prompt: After the swap, can either child at an end of the line say 2?

Both end children can say 2 because they are the tallest or shortest.
Only the tallest child can say 2, and it now stands at an end.
An end child can say 2 when its single neighbour is taller.

why.Both end children can say 2 because they: The shortest child is now between two taller children, not at an end.
why.Only the tallest child can say 2, and it: Being tallest does not make a child taller than both neighbours.
why.An end child can say 2 when its single n: Having one taller neighbour makes the child say 1, not 2.

activities.explanation: A child at an end has only one neighbouring child and therefore cannot have two taller neighbours.

activities.prompt: Children stand in a line from shortest to tallest. Explain how each child gets a number.
activities.answer: Each child counts only the neighbouring children who are taller. In the line from shortest to tallest, each of the first four children has one taller neighbour, so each says 1. The tallest child has no taller neighbour, so that child says 0.
points: Count only the taller children next to it.
The first four children each say 1.
The tallest child says 0.
The number shows how many taller children are next to it.
activities.explanation: Check your answer with these points.

Finally, they use 248, 653, 356, 815 and 833 to explore numbers with digit sum 14 and try making such numbers increasingly large.

why.The nine one-digit numbers all share one: Different numbers cannot occupy the same place.

activities.explanation: One-digit numbers occupy consecutive starting places.

activities.context: A class is preparing a number-line activity in which eleven numbers must be placed in their correct positions. Students begin at 1, 2, 3 and continue onwards, so the nine one-digit numbers come first. They then find digit sums for 68, 176 and 545 and discover that all three sums are the same. Finally, they use 248, 653, 356, 815 and 833 to explore numbers with digit sum 14 and try making such numbers increasingly large.
activities.prompt: Each number has a digit sum of 14. Which list goes from smallest to largest?
activities.explanation: Each number is bigger than the one before it.

activities.prompt: Explain how a digit sum is different from placing a number on a number line.
activities.answer: A digit sum is the total obtained by adding the digits of a number. The digit sums of 68, 176 and 545 are equal. Number-line placement is different: each number goes in its correct position among numbers written from 1, 2, 3 onwards.
points: Says a digit sum is the total of all the digits.
Says 68, 176 and 545 have the same digit sum.
Says a number line puts each number in its correct position.
Says the number line starts at 1, 2, 3 and goes on.
activities.explanation: Check your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Manish is comparing his birthday date, 20/12/2012, with Meghana’s birthday date, 11/02/2011, while thinking about clock patterns and calendars. A usual 12-hour clock can show times with matching digit patterns. Last year’s calendar was different from this year’s calendar. A calendar can repeat after six years when only one leap year is included, but after five years when two leap years are included. Manish also checks which thousands can be made in the mental-maths activity.
activities.prompt: What changes if the calendar comparison includes two leap years instead of one?
options: It would repeat one year sooner.
It would repeat one year later.
It would repeat two years later.
It would repeat at the same time.

One leap year gives a six-year repeat period.
The number of leap years is mistaken for added time.
The different repeat periods are treated as unchanged.

activities.explanation: Two leap years give a five-year repeat period.

activities.context: Manish is comparing his birthday date, 20/12/2012, with Meghana’s birthday date, 11/02/2011, while thinking about clock patterns and calendars. A usual 12-hour clock can show times with matching digit patterns. Last year’s calendar was different from this year’s calendar. A calendar can repeat after six years when only one leap year is included, but after five years when two leap years are included. Manish also checks which thousands can be made in the mental-maths activity.
activities.prompt: Meghana wants a difference made by adding and subtracting 25,000, 400 and 13,000 in the boxes. Which result should she accept?

why.38,800: 38,800 is a number that can be made, but it is not the stated difference.
why.16,000: 16,000 is one of the sums, not the stated difference.
why.1,000: 1,000 is the only thousand that cannot be made.

activities.explanation: 39,800 is the stated difference made by adding and subtracting the box numbers.

activities.prompt: Explain why including two leap years makes the calendar repeat sooner than including only one leap year.
activities.answer: A calendar pattern with one leap year repeats after six years. If two leap years are included, the pattern repeats after five years. Therefore, changing the pattern from one leap year to two makes the calendar repeat one year sooner, rather than at the same time.
points: States the six-year period for one leap year.
States the five-year period for two leap years.
Explains that the period becomes one year shorter.
Compares the two calendar patterns clearly.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a mathematics activity, Paromita looked at a number-pattern display. One row showed eight 32s. The class also tried Collatz sequences and learned how even and odd terms change. Later, the students played two number games: one used additions of 1, 2, or 3, while the other allowed additions from 1 to 10. Paromita estimated that about 100 children were in the class because an exact count was not needed.
activities.prompt: A Collatz sequence reaches an even term. What should the student do next?
options: Divide that term by two.
Multiply that term by 3, then add 1.
Add 1 to that term.
Leave that term unchanged.

That is the rule for an odd term.
The even-number rule does not use addition.
Each Collatz step changes the current term.

activities.explanation: This matches the rule for even terms.

activities.context: During a mathematics activity, Paromita looked at a number-pattern display. One row showed eight 32s. The class also tried Collatz sequences and learned how even and odd terms change. Later, the students played two number games: one used additions of 1, 2, or 3, while the other allowed additions from 1 to 10. Paromita estimated that about 100 children were in the class because an exact count was not needed.
activities.prompt: Why is Paromita's estimate of about 100 children suitable in the case?
options: About 100 is enough when the exact count is not needed.
About 100 means the class has exactly 100 children.
About 100 is useful only for finding number patterns.
About 100 is useful only for playing the number games.

why.About 100 is useful only for playing the: Estimates are not limited to number games.

activities.explanation: The situation does not require an exact count.

activities.prompt: How does forming and following orderly steps in the number games show computational thinking?
activities.answer: Computational thinking means forming orderly steps to use numbers. In the first game, the step is to add 1, 2, or 3 to the previous number. In the second game, the step is to add a number from 1 to 10. These clear rules guide each player's next move.
points: Names orderly steps as computational thinking
Gives the first game's addition choices
Gives the second game's addition range
Explains that the rules guide players

chapters.title: Data Handling and Presentation
chapters.summary: In this chapter: lesson 1: what data is and how we organise it; lesson 2: understanding pictographs; lesson 3: reading bar graphs; lesson 4: drawing bar graphs.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What Data Is and How We Organise It

activities.prompt: How can we turn classmates’ choices into useful information?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Data
activities.body:
You explore your classroom. You wonder what data is and how people organise it. Data means facts, numbers, measures, observations or descriptions that give information.

A list of classmates’ favourite colours is one example. Navya and Naresh also visited every student. They asked about favourite games.

Now meet Shri Nilesh. He made one tally mark for every student naming a sweet. When five marks appeared, he crossed the first four.

The numbers 6, 9 and so on show the frequencies. These tell how many students chose each sweet. The sweets table helped Shri Nilesh buy the correct number of each sweet.

Then Sandhya arranged students’ shoe sizes from smallest to largest. Ordered data makes it easy to count how often each value occurs. Shoe-size data can also appear in a frequency table.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Understanding Data
activities.body: Data gives us information. It can have facts, numbers, measures, observations and descriptions. A class survey about favourite games is data. Tally marks can show how many people chose each sweet. A frequency table shows how often each answer happens. Ordered data puts values in order, like shoe sizes from smallest to largest. This helps us count values. These simple ways make class information easy to read and use.
keyPoints: Data gives information about a group.
Tally marks and frequency tables help us count answers.
Ordered data makes repeated values easier to count.
activities.explanation: These ways turn class information into useful facts.

activities.title: Ordering Data and Using a Frequency Table
activities.body: Ordered data places values in a clear sequence. Sandhya arranged shoe sizes from smallest to largest. This order helps us count how often each size occurs. The same shoe-size data can also go into a frequency table. A frequency table records how often each value appears, so patterns become easier to see.
keyPoints: Ordered data places values in sequence.
A frequency table shows how often each value occurs.
Both methods make repeated values easier to count.
activities.explanation: Ordering and frequency tables both make repeated values easier to count.

activities.title: What Is Data?
activities.prompt: A collection of facts or information is called ______.
activities.hint: Think of the list of classmates’ favourite colours.
activities.explanation: The favourite-colour list is data because it gives information.

activities.title: A Favourite Games Survey
activities.prompt: Navya and Naresh asked every student about favourite games.
activities.explanation: They went to each student in the class to ask this question.

activities.title: Match Each Example
activities.prompt: Match each example with the information it shows.
pairs: One student who named a sweet
The correct number of each sweet to buy
activities.explanation: Each example matches with the information it provides.

activities.title: Order the Sweet Survey Steps
activities.prompt: Put these actions in the order they happen in the sweet survey.
items: Make one tally mark for each student who named a sweet.
When the count reaches five, put a line through the first four marks.
Read the frequencies of the sweet preferences.
Buy the correct number of each sweet.
activities.explanation: The tally count comes first, followed by the frequencies and buying step.

activities.prompt: Navya and Naresh asked 20 students about their favourite games. How many game preferences did they record?
activities.explanation: One preference was recorded for each student, so the formula is n+0. With n=20, 20+0=20 game preferences.

activities.prompt: Shri Nilesh made 6 tally marks for the students who named a sweet. How many tally marks did he make?
activities.explanation: He made one tally mark for each student, so the formula is n+0. With n=6, 6+0=6 tally marks.

activities.prompt: A tally has 2 crossed groups of five marks and 1 extra marks. How many students named the sweet?
activities.explanation: Each crossed group has 5 marks, so the formula is 5*g+r. With g=2 and r=1, 5*2+1=11 students.

activities.prompt: A frequency table shows this: 10 students chose laddoos. 4 students chose barfis. How many more students chose laddoos than barfis?
activities.explanation: Subtract the smaller number from the bigger number: a-b. With a = 8 and b = 2, 8-2 = 6 students.

activities.prompt: Sandhya lines up these shoe sizes: 7 cm, 10 cm, 13 cm. What is the difference between the biggest and smallest size in cm?
activities.explanation: The biggest size is l. The smallest is s. So the formula is l-s. With l=11 and s=5, 11-5=6 cm.

activities.prompt: A shoe-size frequency table (a table of counts) shows 4 students in one size group. It shows 3 students in another size group. How many students are in the table in all?
activities.explanation: Add the frequencies (the counts) to find the total. The formula is a+b. With a=4 and b=3, 4+3=7 students.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reading Bar Graphs

activities.prompt: How can a bar graph help you read traffic information?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Reading the Delhi Traffic Graph
activities.body:
Imagine you stand at a Delhi crossing, wanting to know when most vehicles passed. A bar graph helps you understand and interpret the information quickly. For lots of data, preparing a pictograph takes a lot of time. A pictograph can also be difficult to prepare with lots of data. So, you choose bars for your display.

Bar graphs can have uniform-width bars. These bars may be drawn horizontally or vertically. On this graph, the horizontal lines are equally spaced. When the frequencies are large, a scale or key is useful.

In the Delhi traffic graph, one unit of length stands for 100 vehicles. The longest bar shows the maximum traffic. This happened from 7 to 8 a.m. So, about 1200 vehicles passed through the crossing then.

Now find the smallest bar. It shows the minimum traffic, which occurred from 6 to 7 a.m. About 150 vehicles passed through the crossing during that hour. By comparing bar lengths and using the scale, you can read both values quickly.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Bar graphs at a glance
activities.body: Bar graphs help us quickly understand and interpret information. Their bars are all the same width and may be horizontal or vertical. The horizontal lines are equally spaced. A scale or key helps when the counts are large. In the Delhi traffic graph, one unit of length stands for 100 vehicles. The longest bar shows maximum traffic, while the smallest bar shows minimum traffic.
keyPoints: Bar graphs help us understand information quickly.
Bars have equal width and may be horizontal or vertical.
A scale or key helps when counts are large.
The longest bar shows maximum traffic.
activities.explanation: Bar graphs turn information into bars that we can compare easily.

activities.title: Change the bars

tasks.then: The tallest bar shows the biggest count.

tasks.say: Change the scale so one mark stands for 10.
tasks.then: A scale changes the marks, not the data.

activities.takeaway: A bar graph lets us compare at a glance.
activities.explanation: A bar graph lets us compare at a glance.

activities.title: Ways to draw bars
activities.prompt: Bar graph bars may be drawn horizontally or vertically.
activities.explanation: Bar graphs can have bars drawn in either direction.

activities.title: Using a scale
activities.prompt: A scale or key is useful when the counts are ______.
activities.hint: Think of a market with many things to count.
activities.explanation: A scale or key is useful when there are many items to count.

activities.title: Match the traffic facts
activities.prompt: Match each traffic fact with its correct value or time.
activities.explanation: These pairs match the Delhi graph's scale, times, and traffic amounts.

activities.prompt: A vertical bar is 2 cm long. At 10 marbles for each centimetre, how many marbles does it show?
activities.explanation: Multiply the bar length by 10: b*10 marbles.

activities.prompt: A horizontal bar is 3 cm long. Each centimetre represents 5 buses. How many buses does the bar show?
activities.explanation: Multiply the bar length by 5: b*5 buses. Add 5, subtract 5 from 5, or divide by 5 to make common mistakes.

activities.prompt: A bar graph has 4 vertical bars. Every bar is 6 cm wide. What is the total width of all the bars in cm?
activities.explanation: Multiply the number of bars by the width of each bar: n*w cm.

activities.prompt: A bar graph has 3 flat (horizontal) lines. The bottom line and the top line are two of them. The lines are the same distance apart. How many equal spaces are between the lines?
activities.explanation: The number of spaces is one less than the number of lines: n-1.

activities.prompt: The longest bar in a traffic graph is 12 units long. One unit of length stands for 100 vehicles. How many vehicles does the longest bar show?
activities.explanation: Multiply the longest bar length by 100: b*100 vehicles. The longest bar shows the maximum traffic.

activities.title: Compare two bars
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order. Compare the shortest bar and the longest bar.
items: Read the traffic at 6 to 7 a.m.
Read the traffic at 7 to 8 a.m.
activities.explanation: The shortest bar shows the least traffic from 6 to 7 a.m. The longest bar shows the most traffic from 7 to 8 a.m.

activities.prompt: The smallest bar in a traffic graph is 3 units long. One unit of length stands for 100 vehicles. How many vehicles does the smallest bar show?
activities.explanation: Multiply the smallest bar length by 100: b*100 vehicles. The smallest bar shows the minimum traffic.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Drawing Bar Graphs

activities.prompt: How can you turn a sweets table into a bar graph?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Bar Graphs from Sweets and Scores
activities.body:
You arrive at a sweets table with a list of sweets and their frequencies. You wonder how to show this information as a clear bar graph. Let us begin together, step by step.

First, write the names of the sweets along the horizontal line with equal spacing. Next, write the frequencies along the vertical line. Before drawing any bars, choose a suitable scale.

For this sweets table, one unit of length can represent one student. The jalebi bar must have a height of six units. Draw every other bar as high as its frequency.

Now turn to Smriti’s match scores. Here, one unit of length can represent ten runs. Mark the scale on the vertical line and draw the bars for the scores.

You also need a suitable scale along the vertical line for this graph. Make sure the unit markings begin from zero. Draw all bars with the same width and a uniform gap between them.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How to draw a bar graph
activities.body: For the sweets graph, write the sweet names along the horizontal line with equal spacing. Write the frequencies along the vertical line. Choose a suitable scale before drawing the bars. One unit can represent one student in the sweets table. The jalebi bar must be six units high. For Smriti’s match scores, one unit can represent ten runs. Mark the scale on the vertical line.
keyPoints: Sweet names go on the horizontal line with equal spacing.
Frequencies go on the vertical line.
Choose a suitable scale before drawing the bars.
activities.explanation: A bar graph becomes clear when its lines, scale, and bars are drawn carefully.

activities.title: Change the bars

tasks.then: The tallest bar shows the biggest count.

tasks.say: Change the scale so one mark stands for 10.
tasks.then: A scale changes the marks, not the data.

activities.takeaway: A bar graph lets us compare at a glance.
activities.explanation: A bar graph lets us compare at a glance.

activities.title: Where do frequencies go?
activities.prompt: Along which line should you write the frequencies?
options: The horizontal line
The vertical line
The gap between bars
The sweet names
activities.explanation: Write the frequencies along the vertical line. This shows the heights for the bars.

activities.title: Spacing the sweet names
activities.prompt: Sweet names should have equal spacing along the horizontal line.
activities.explanation: Yes. Equal spacing keeps the horizontal line neat and easy to read.

activities.title: Smriti’s scale
activities.prompt: For Smriti’s match scores, one unit of length can represent ______ runs.
activities.hint: Look at the scale used for match scores.
activities.explanation: For Smriti’s match scores, one unit of length can represent ten runs.

activities.title: Match the graph parts
activities.prompt: Match each graph part with its correct place or meaning.
activities.explanation: The names and frequencies belong on different lines. The scale must suit the data.

activities.prompt: There are 5 sweet names along the horizontal line. How many equal gaps are needed between the names?
activities.explanation: There is one fewer gap than there are sweet names, so (n-1) = 4 equal gaps.

activities.prompt: A sweet was chosen by 3 students. What frequency should be written for that sweet on the vertical line?
activities.explanation: The frequency is the number of students, so f*1 = 3 students.

activities.prompt: A sweet other than jalebi was chosen by 5 students. One unit of length represents one student. How high should its bar be in scale units?
activities.explanation: One unit represents one student, so f*1 = 5 scale units.

activities.prompt: The jalebi bar must be six units high. Another sweet was chosen by 4 students, so its bar is 4 units high. How many units higher is the jalebi bar?
activities.explanation: The difference in bar heights is (6-f) = 2 units.

activities.prompt: The tallest bar has 24 students. The scale starts at zero and has 4 equal units up to the tallest bar. Which scale is suitable: (m/h), (h/m), or (m+h) students per unit?
activities.explanation: Divide the greatest frequency by the number of scale units: (m/h) = 6 students per unit.

activities.prompt: Smriti scored 20 runs. One unit of length represents ten runs. How high should her bar be in scale units?
activities.explanation: Divide the score by ten, so (s/10) = 2 scale units.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Artistic and Aesthetic Considerations

activities.prompt: How can we make mountain heights easier to see and compare?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Choosing a Clear Picture
activities.body:
You arrive at a large table of mountain heights. It is not easy to compare them. First, you choose a suitable scale. This helps control the size of your presentation. It should fit the space where you will display it.

Next, you draw each mountain height as a horizontal box. The mountain bar graph now makes the heights easier to compare at a glance. Your presentation also looks visually appealing. It remains easy to understand.

You also learn about vertical bars. A bar graph with vertical bars is called a column graph. Vertical bars usually suit heights measured upwards from the ground. Horizontal bars usually suit lengths parallel to the ground.

Then you meet an infographic. This is the shortened name for information graphics. In the mountain infographic, taller triangles are also wider.

Finally, you check whether the picture gives a misleading impression. Making a picture more appealing can sometimes mislead people. You choose a suitable scale again. You keep your presentation clear, attractive and easy to understand.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Designing a Clear Data Presentation
activities.body: A good data presentation should fit the space where it will be displayed. Choosing a suitable scale helps control its size. It should also look appealing and be easy to understand. Comparing many mountain heights is difficult from a large table of numbers. A mountain bar graph uses horizontal boxes. The heights are easier to compare at a glance.
keyPoints: Fit the presentation into its display space.
Choose a suitable scale to control its size.
Make the presentation appealing and easy to understand.
activities.explanation: Clear design controls size and supports easy understanding.

activities.title: Bar Directions and Visual Appeal
activities.body: Vertical bars are usually best for showing heights measured upwards from the ground. Horizontal bars are usually best for showing lengths parallel to the ground. Information graphics are shortened to infographics. In the mountain infographic, taller triangles are also wider. Making a picture more appealing can sometimes give people a misleading impression.
keyPoints: Use vertical bars for heights measured upwards.
Use horizontal bars for lengths parallel to the ground.
Check that added appeal does not create a misleading impression.
activities.explanation: Choose the right bar direction and check whether the picture misleads.

activities.prompt: A data presentation should fit the space where it will be displayed.
activities.explanation: Yes. The presentation should fit its display space.

activities.prompt: What helps control the size of a data presentation?
options: Choosing a suitable scale
Using a large table of numbers
Drawing each value as a horizontal box
activities.explanation: A suitable scale helps control the size of a presentation.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct description.
pairs: Heights measured upwards from the ground
activities.explanation: The pairs use the bar directions and names from the lesson.

activities.prompt: A poster chart is 20 cm wide. A 4 cm margin is left on each side. What is the width inside the margins in cm?
activities.explanation: Width inside the margins = poster width - two margins = 20 - 2*4 = 12 cm. This helps the chart fit the available space.

activities.prompt: A bar picture is 18 cm wide when the scale number is 3. The scale number changes to 1. How wide is the picture now, in cm?
activities.explanation: New width = old width × new scale ÷ old scale = 18 × 1 ÷ 3 = 6 cm. The scale number changes the size of the picture.

activities.prompt: A column graph has 4 vertical bars. There is one equal gap of 4 cm between each pair of bars. What is the total width of all the gaps in cm?
activities.explanation: There are 4 - 1 gaps. Total gap width = (4 - 1)*4 = 12 cm. Equal gaps make the infographic easy to understand. Information graphics are shortened to infographics.

activities.prompt: A large table lists 10 mountain heights. Exactly 4 heights are below 2000 m. How many mountain heights in the table are 2000 m or more?
activities.explanation: Heights at or above 2000 m = all listed heights - heights below 2000 m = 10 - 4 = 6 heights.

activities.prompt: The longest bar is 50 cm long. The shortest bar is 10 cm long. How many cm longer is the longest bar than the shortest bar?
activities.explanation: Difference in bar lengths = 50 - 10 = 40 cm. The bars make the lengths easy to compare.

activities.prompt: Put the mountain comparison ideas from harder to easier.
items: Compare heights using a large table
Draw each value as a horizontal box
Compare the mountain bars at a glance
activities.explanation: The table is harder to compare. Horizontal boxes help, and the mountain bar graph makes heights easier to compare.

activities.prompt: A column graph has two vertical columns. One is 30 cm tall and the other is 10 cm tall. What is the sum of their heights in cm?
activities.explanation: Sum of the column heights = 30 + 10 = 40 cm. A bar graph with vertical bars is also called a column graph, and vertical bars show heights measured upwards from the ground.

activities.title: Ordered data
activities.prompt: Ordered data makes it easy to count how often each value occurs.
activities.explanation: Yes! Ordering data helps you count each value more easily.

activities.title: What is data?
activities.prompt: Data is a group of facts, numbers, measures, ______ or descriptions. They give information.
activities.hint: Think about what you notice and write down.
activities.explanation: Well done! Observations are things you notice and write down.

activities.title: Match each idea
activities.prompt: Match each idea on the left with its correct meaning.
pairs: count how often each value occurs
activities.explanation: Excellent! You matched each idea with its correct meaning.

activities.title: Draw a sweets bar graph
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.

chapters.title: Prime Time
chapters.summary: In this chapter: common multiples and common factors; prime numbers; co-prime numbers for safekeeping treasures; prime factorisation.

lessons.title: Common Multiples and Common Factors

activities.prompt: How can a number game help you spot hidden links?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Number Games and Number Links
activities.body:
Imagine you join a number game. Instead of saying multiples of 3, you say “idli”. Instead of saying multiples of 5, you say “vada”. A number fitting both rules gets the name “idli-vada”.

The first special call is 15. You keep playing and discover more numbers like it. These are common multiples. Each one is a multiple of both 3 and 5.

Now you tour 24. Its factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24. You can land on 24 with jumps of 2, 3, 6, 8 or 12. Each jump size is a factor too.

Next, imagine treasures labelled 14 and 36. You look for jumps reaching both. The answers are 1 and 2. These are their common factors. Such jumps are common factors.

Finally, you meet a perfect number. Its factors add up to twice the number. This rule helps you recognise it.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Playing with Multiples and Factors
activities.body: In the idli-vada game, players say “idli” for multiples of 3 and “vada” for multiples of 5. A multiple of both gets the name “idli-vada”. The first such number is 15. Numbers like this are common multiples. Common factors are jump sizes that reach both treasures. For 14 and 36, these are 1 and 2. A perfect number has factors whose sum is twice the number.
keyPoints: Common multiples are multiples of both 3 and 5.
Common factors reach both treasures.
Perfect numbers have factors that sum to twice the number.
activities.explanation: The game shows how numbers can share the same multiple or factor.

activities.prompt: In the idli-vada game, players say “vada” for multiples of 3.
activities.explanation: Players say “idli” for multiples of 3. They say “vada” for multiples of 5.

activities.prompt: Match each number group with its game name.
activities.explanation: The game uses each name for its matching group of multiples.

activities.prompt: Put these factors of 24 in increasing order.
activities.explanation: These listed factors of 24 are already arranged from smallest to largest.

activities.prompt: A shop packs 30 idlis into groups of 3 idlis. How many groups are there?
activities.explanation: Each group has 3 idlis, so the number of groups is 30/3. For example, 12 idlis make 4 groups.

activities.prompt: A shop packs 30 vadas into groups of 5 vadas. How many groups are there?
activities.explanation: Each group has 5 vadas, so the number of groups is 30/5. For example, 20 vadas make 4 groups.

activities.prompt: How many idli-vada numbers are there from 1 to 45? Choose one: 45/15, 45/3, or 45/5.
activities.explanation: An idli-vada number is a multiple of both 3 and 5. These common multiples are 15, 30, 45, and so on, so the number up to 45 is 45/15.

activities.prompt: The first common multiple of 3 and 5 is 15. What is the 4th common multiple of 3 and 5?
activities.explanation: The common multiples are 15, 30, 45, and so on. Therefore, the 4th common multiple is 4*15.

activities.prompt: A bag has 24 marbles shared equally among 1 children. How many marbles does each child get?
activities.explanation: The jump sizes 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6 can all reach 24. Thus, 24 marbles shared among 1 children give 24/1 marbles per child.

activities.prompt: Which pair lists the common factors of 14 and 36?
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
activities.explanation: The common factors of 14 and 36 are exactly 1 and 2.

activities.prompt: A jump size of 4 cm can land on 24 cm. If a marble makes 3 such jumps, how many cm does it travel? Choose one: 4*3, 4+3, or 3/4.
activities.explanation: Each jump covers 4 cm, so 3 jumps cover 4*3 cm.

lessons.title: Prime Numbers

activities.prompt: Ready to find the prime numbers hiding in a sieve?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Prime Number Journey
activities.body:
You begin with an arrangement of figs. Its rows and columns multiply to give 12. You also notice that they are factors of 12. For 7 figs, there is only one rectangular arrangement possible.

Now you use a sieve to find prime numbers. Prime numbers have exactly two factors, namely 1 and themselves. The first few prime numbers are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19.

Each of these numbers has factors 1 and the number itself. You circle the prime numbers in the sieve. All the circled numbers are prime numbers. You see that all the crossed-out numbers except 1 are composite numbers.

Numbers with more than two factors are called composite numbers. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite. This method of finding primes is called the Sieve of Eratosthenes.

Before you leave, you spot two pairs. 11 and 13 are twin primes. 17 and 19 are twin primes too.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What is a prime number?
activities.body: Prime numbers have exactly two factors: 1 and the number itself. The first few prime numbers are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite. Numbers with more than two factors are called composite numbers. You can find primes by crossing out numbers in a sieve. This method is called the Sieve of Eratosthenes.
keyPoints: Prime numbers have exactly two factors: 1 and themselves.
The first primes are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19.
The number 1 is neither prime nor composite.
activities.explanation: You can spot primes by checking whether they have exactly two factors.

activities.prompt: The number 1 is a prime number.
activities.explanation: The number 1 is neither prime nor composite. It does not have exactly two factors.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with its correct term.
activities.explanation: Prime numbers have two factors. Composite numbers have more than two factors.

activities.prompt: Put these prime numbers in increasing order.
activities.explanation: This is the given order of the first few prime numbers.

activities.prompt: In a sieve, what are the crossed-out numbers, except 1?
options: Composite numbers
Prime numbers
Twin primes
Numbers in rectangle shapes
activities.explanation: The crossed-out numbers, except 1, are composite numbers.

activities.prompt: For 7 prime figs, the rectangular arrangement has one row. How many figs are in that row?
activities.explanation: Number of figs = 7 / 1 = 7 figs. For 7 figs, the only rectangular arrangement is 1 row of 7 figs.

activities.prompt: What is the sum of the two factors of the prime number 7?
activities.explanation: The factors are 1 and 7. Their sum is 1 + 7 = 8.

activities.prompt: A composite number has more than two factors. What is the least number of factors it can have?
activities.explanation: More than 2 means at least 3 factors. The formula gives 4/4 + 2 = 3.

activities.prompt: A sieve goes from 1 to 21. How many numbers are crossed out, except 1?
activities.explanation: There are 21 numbers. Take away 1 and the 8 primes from 2 to 19. 21 - 1 - 8 = 12.

activities.prompt: The numbers 3 and 3 are two of the first few prime numbers. What is their sum?
activities.explanation: Both numbers are prime numbers. Their sum is 3 + 3 = 6.

lessons.title: Co-prime Numbers for Safekeeping Treasures

activities.prompt: Can two numbers guard a treasure together without sharing a factor?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Guarding Treasures Together
activities.body:
You arrive at a new treasure game. A jump size of 1 is not allowed. You try the pair 4 and 9. No allowed jump size reaches both numbers. So this pair is safe.

Now you look for common factors. Safe pairs have no common factor other than 1. Numbers with no common factor other than 1 are called co-prime. So 4 and 9 are co-prime.

Next you test 15 and 39. These numbers are not co-prime. The reason is that 3 divides both.

You then explore common multiples. Sometimes the first common multiple equals the product of the numbers. At other times it is less than the product.

Finally, you visit some thread diagrams. One diagram has 13 pegs and a thread-gap of 3. In some diagrams, the thread is tied to every peg. You finish by checking common factors carefully.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Safe Treasure Pairs
activities.body: In this treasure game, a jump size of 1 is not allowed. A safe pair has no common factor other than 1. Two numbers like this are called co-prime. The pair 4 and 9 is safe and co-prime. The pair 15 and 39 is not co-prime because 3 divides both. Sometimes, the first common multiple equals the product. At other times, it is less than the product.
keyPoints: Safe pairs have no common factor other than 1.
The pair 4 and 9 is co-prime.
The pair 15 and 39 is not co-prime.
activities.explanation: Co-prime numbers help treasure guides keep safe pairs.

activities.prompt: A jump size of 1 is allowed in the new treasure game.
activities.explanation: The new treasure game does not allow a jump size of 1.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with its correct detail.
pairs: thread is tied to every peg
activities.explanation: Each pair repeats a fact from the sheet.

activities.prompt: Why are 15 and 39 not co-prime?
options: 3 divides both numbers.
No factor is shared.
The product is smaller.
The first common multiple is the product.
activities.explanation: The number 3 divides both 15 and 39. They share a common factor.

activities.prompt: Put these ideas in a clear thinking order.
items: 15 and 39 share a common factor other than 1.
activities.explanation: Start with the shared factor. Then use the co-prime rule.

activities.prompt: A checker takes 2 marbles away from 2 marbles and adds one marble for the common group. How many marbles are in the common group of a safe pair?
activities.explanation: The common group has (4-4)+1 = 1 marble. A safe pair has no common factor other than 1.

activities.prompt: A treasure pair has 3*4 marbles and 3*3 marbles. If 3 is used as a common jump size, how many groups of 3 marbles are there in the two piles together?
activities.explanation: The total number of groups is (d*x/d)+(d*y/d). The common jump size 3 fits into both piles.

activities.prompt: The treasure piles have 45 marbles and 78 marbles, and 3 divides both numbers. How many groups of 3 marbles are there in the two piles together?
activities.explanation: Divide each pile by 3 and add the group counts: (15/3)+(39/3) = 18 groups. The numbers 15 and 39 are not co-prime because 3 divides both.

activities.prompt: A co-prime treasure pair has 4 marbles and 3 marbles. What is their first common multiple in marbles?
activities.explanation: For the pair 2 and 3, the first common multiple is 2*3 = 6 marbles. For co-prime numbers, the first common multiple is their product.

activities.prompt: A thread is tied to every one of 10 pegs. Each peg costs 5 rupees. How many rupees are needed for all the pegs?
activities.explanation: Multiply the number of pegs by the cost of one peg: 13*2 = 26 rupees.

lessons.sceneCaption: Co-prime treasures share only the blocked factor 1!
