lessons.title: Prime Factorisation

activities.prompt: Can you discover the secret building blocks inside a number?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Prime Factor Tour
activities.body:
Imagine you meet 56. You want its factors, but showing one factorisation may not reveal all of them.

Prime factorisation means writing a number as a product of prime numbers. The prime factors in this prime factorisation are called prime factors. For 56, you find the prime factorisation: 2 × 2 × 2 × 7.

Every number greater than 1 has a prime factorisation. The number 1 does not have a prime factorisation. You try the prime number 7, and its prime factorisation is just 7. A number has only one prime factorisation, apart from the order of its factors. The order of the prime factors does not matter.

Next, you look for common prime factors. Two numbers are co-prime when they have no common prime factors. A systematic method helps you check this.

Finally, you compare prime factorisations for divisibility. One number is divisible by another when its prime factorisation includes the other factorisation.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What is prime factorisation?
activities.body: Prime factorisation means writing a number as a product of prime numbers. For 56, it is 2 × 2 × 2 × 7. The order of these prime factors does not matter. Every number greater than 1 has a prime factorisation, but 1 does not. The prime number 7 has the prime factorisation 7. Two numbers are co-prime when they have no common prime factors.
keyPoints: Prime factorisation uses a product of prime numbers.
The prime factorisation of 56 is 2 × 2 × 2 × 7.
Co-prime numbers have no common prime factors.
activities.explanation: Prime factors help us compare numbers systematically.

activities.title: Find the prime factorisation
activities.prompt: Which is the prime factorisation of 56?
activities.explanation: The prime factors of 56 are 2, 2, 2 and 7.

activities.title: Prime number 7
activities.prompt: The prime factorisation of the prime number 7 is just ______.
activities.hint: It is the prime number itself.
activities.explanation: the lesson gives the prime factorisation of 7 as just 7.

activities.title: Match each idea
activities.prompt: Match each idea to its meaning.
pairs: Writing a number as a product of prime numbers
Numbers with no common prime factors
A number without a prime factorisation
activities.explanation: Each pair joins an idea with its meaning from the facts.

activities.prompt: A shop has 3 boxes. Each box has 7 laddoos. Write the total as prime factors multiplied together. How many laddoos are there?
activities.explanation: Multiply the prime factors to get the number of laddoos: p * q.

activities.prompt: The prime factorisation of the number of marbles is 2 * 2 * 3. How many marbles are there?
activities.explanation: Repeated prime factors are also multiplied, so the number of marbles is p * p * q.

activities.prompt: Two children write the prime factors of 6 marbles as 3 * 7 and 7 * 3. What is the number of marbles?
activities.explanation: The order of prime factors does not matter. Both factorisations give the same number of marbles.

activities.prompt: 3 is a prime number. What prime number does its prime factorisation show?
activities.explanation: The prime factorisation of a prime number is the prime number itself.

lessons.sceneAlt: A diagram shows 56 becoming the prime factors 2, 2, 2 and 7, shows that rearranging those factors changes nothing, compares the prime factors 7 and 2 in circles with an empty overlap to show they are co-prime, and notes that 1 has no prime factorisation.
lessons.sceneCaption: Prime factors split a number into primes, and co-prime numbers have no prime factor in common.

lessons.title: Divisibility Tests

activities.prompt: Can you spot the secret clues that make some numbers divide neatly?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Clues in the Digits
activities.body:
You begin with a number and wonder whether long division is really necessary. The answer is no. Quick tests can often tell you what you need to know.

First, check the final digit. A 0 shows that the number is divisible by 10. A 0 or 5 shows that it is divisible by 5. For divisibility by 2, look for 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.

Now try divisibility by 4. The last digit alone cannot show it. Only the last two digits matter. Take 8536. Its final two digits make 36. Since 36 is divisible by 4, so is 8536.

Next comes divisibility by 8. Only the last three digits matter here. Those digits must form a multiple of 8. If they do, the whole number is divisible by 8. These quick checks spare you from always using long division.

You can also apply divisibility to years. Leap years usually occur in multiples of 4. For example, 2024 is a leap year because February has 29 days. Now you have handy tests for many divisibility questions.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Quick divisibility checks
activities.body: Sometimes, skip long division. A number divisible by 10 ends in 0. One divisible by 5 ends in 0 or 5. One divisible by 2 ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. For 4, only the last two digits matter. For 8, only the last three digits matter. Leap years are usually in multiples of 4. The year 2024 is a leap year because February has 29 days.
keyPoints: Divisible by 10, 5 or 2? Check the last digit.
Divisible by 4? Check the last two digits.
Divisible by 8? Check the last three digits.
activities.explanation: These digit checks can replace long division for the rules shown.

activities.title: Divisible by 10
activities.prompt: Which ending shows that a number is divisible by 10?
activities.explanation: Good choice! A number divisible by 10 ends in 0.

activities.title: Divisible by 5
activities.prompt: A number divisible by 5 must end in 0.
activities.explanation: Nice try! A number divisible by 5 ends in either 0 or 5.

activities.title: Divisible by 2
activities.prompt: A number ends in 6. Is it divisible by 2?
options: Yes
No
Only sometimes
We cannot tell
activities.explanation: Yes! A number divisible by 2 can end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.

activities.title: Checking divisibility by 4
activities.prompt: Only the last ______ digits matter when checking divisibility by 4.
activities.hint: Look at the ending, not the whole number.
activities.explanation: Great! The last two digits alone are enough for this check.

activities.title: Match each divisibility test
activities.prompt: Match each divisibility test with its rule.
pairs: only the last two digits matter
activities.explanation: Well done! Each test uses the digit or digits shown here.

activities.title: Check 8536
activities.prompt: Why is 8536 divisible by 4?
options: Only its last digit proves it.
36 is divisible by 4.
Only its first two digits matter.
No divisibility test is needed.
activities.explanation: Great! Only the last two digits matter. Here, 36 is divisible by 4.

activities.title: Check divisibility by 8
activities.prompt: Put the steps for checking divisibility by 8 in order.
items: Look at the last three digits.
Check whether they form a multiple of 8.
Decide if the whole number is divisible by 8.
activities.explanation: Perfect! The last three digits must form a multiple of 8.

activities.title: Why is 2024 a leap year?
activities.prompt: Which sentence explains why 2024 is a leap year?
options: Its last digit is enough.
Long division is always needed.
It is a multiple of 10.
February has 29 days.
activities.explanation: Yes! February has 29 days. Leap years usually occur in multiples of 4.

lessons.sceneCaption: Check divisibility by looking at special digits instead of doing long division.

lessons.title: Fun with Numbers

activities.prompt: Can you discover why some numbers are special in their boxes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Number Mysteries
activities.body:
You meet 9, 25 and 43 during your number tour. You begin with 9. It is special because it has only one digit. In the first box, 9 is the only multiple of 3.

Now look at 25. It is special because it is the only multiple of 5. Next, you meet 43. It is the only prime number in its box. You notice that 43 is also the only number there that is not a square.

Next, you enter the prime puzzle. You must fill it with prime numbers only. The product of each column must equal the number below that column. You check each column before comparing products.

Now you discover factors. If one number divides another, the second number is a factor of the first. You try this idea on numbers around you. A composite number has more than two factors.

Finally, you learn prime factorisation. You can write a number as a product of prime numbers. This is called prime factorisation. Each number has only one prime factorisation apart from the order of its factors.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Special Number Clues
activities.body: The number 9 has one digit and is the first box's only multiple of 3. The number 25 is the only multiple of 5. The number 43 is the only prime and only number not square in its box. A composite has more than two factors. Prime puzzles use prime numbers only. Each column's product must equal the number below it. Prime factorisation writes a number as prime factors.
keyPoints: Numbers 9, 25, and 43 have special clues.
A factor divides another number; composites have more than two factors.
Prime factorisation stays the same apart from factor order.
activities.explanation: These clues help you sort numbers and describe their factors.

one digit
no digits
only one factor
activities.explanation: The number 9 is special because it has only one digit.

Check the number below each column
activities.explanation: Fill the puzzle with primes, multiply each column, then check the number below.

activities.prompt: A shop gives a customer 9 rupees and then 10 more rupees. What is the total amount in rupees?
activities.explanation: Total amount = 9 + n, so the answer is in rupees.

activities.prompt: In the first box, 9 is the only multiple of 3. If 6 laddoos are put into groups of 3, how many groups are made?
activities.explanation: Number of groups = n / 3.

activities.prompt: The number 25 is the only multiple of 5. If 20 laddoos are put into rows of 5, how many rows are made?
activities.explanation: Number of rows = n / 5.

activities.prompt: The only number in a box that is not a square is 43. A square cloth has side 3 cm. What is its area in square cm?
activities.explanation: Area of the square = s * s square cm.

activities.prompt: A number is written as the product of the prime factors 5 and 3. What is the number?
activities.explanation: Prime factorisation = p * q, so the product is the number.

chapters.title: Perimeter and Area
chapters.summary: In this chapter: perimeter of rectangles, squares and triangles; tracks and regular polygons; understanding area; estimating area with squares.

lessons.title: Perimeter of rectangles, squares and triangles

activities.prompt: How can you discover the distance around different shapes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Around Shapes
activities.body:
Imagine you are starting a journey around shapes. You step along each edge and return to your starting point. The distance covered around the boundary is called the perimeter.

First, you meet a polygon. It is a closed plane figure made from line segments. To find its perimeter, add the lengths of all its sides.

Next, you visit a rectangle. Its perimeter is twice the sum of its length and breadth.

A square comes next. Its perimeter is four times the length of one side. Then you meet a triangle, where you add its three side lengths.

Now, picture Akshi’s rectangular tablecloth. Akshi needs 10 m of lace for it. In Usha’s square park, one complete round covers 300 m. Usha travels 900 m when she takes three rounds. You can see how the boundary and its sides work together.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Finding the distance around a shape
activities.body: Perimeter is the distance covered around a closed plane figure. A polygon is made from line segments. Add all side lengths to find its perimeter. For a rectangle, multiply the sum of length and breadth by two. For a square, multiply one side’s length by four. For a triangle, add its three side lengths.
keyPoints: Perimeter is the distance around a closed plane figure.
A polygon’s perimeter is the sum of all its side lengths.
Rectangles, squares and triangles have different perimeter rules.
activities.explanation: Use the rule for the shape you are measuring.

lessons.title: Tracks and regular polygons

activities.prompt: What will you discover as you compare tracks and explore regular polygons?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Comparing Tracks and Polygons
activities.body:
You begin at Akshi’s outer track, where one complete round stretches 220 m. Akshi’s track has a length of 70 m and a breadth of 40 m. Now imagine walking five complete rounds. Akshi covers 1100 m during those five rounds.

Next, you visit Toshi’s inner track, whose perimeter measures 180 m. After seven rounds, Toshi has covered 1260 m. Compare the two totals carefully. Toshi runs a longer distance than Akshi. Which runner travelled farther? The answer is Toshi.

Next, you explore regular polygons. Each has all its sides equal, and all its angles are equal too. You also inspect an equilateral triangle. Its perimeter is three times the length of one side. That simple pattern helps you understand the shape.

You then inspect the first arrangement of two paper pieces. Its perimeter measures 28 cm. You write down the value. The tracks and shapes provide different measurements to compare.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Understanding tracks and regular polygons
activities.body: A round is one complete trip around a track. The perimeter is the distance around a shape. Akshi’s outer track covers 220 m in one round. Toshi’s inner track has a perimeter of 180 m. A regular polygon has all sides and all angles equal. An equilateral triangle has three equal sides, so its perimeter is three times one side length.
keyPoints: A complete round on Akshi’s outer track covers 220 m.
Regular polygons have all sides and all angles equal.
An equilateral triangle’s perimeter is three times one side length.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you compare tracks and work out polygon perimeters.

activities.prompt: How far does one complete round on Akshi’s outer track cover?
activities.explanation: One complete round on Akshi’s outer track covers 220 m. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Match each track fact to its measurement.
pairs: Akshi’s outer track in one complete round
activities.explanation: You matched each track measurement correctly. Great work!

activities.explanation: The perimeter is 2 * (15 + 6) = 42 cm.

activities.prompt: A regular polygon has 4 equal sides, and each side is 5 cm long. What is its perimeter in cm?
activities.explanation: Add all 4 equal sides: 4 * 5 = 20 cm.

activities.prompt: An equilateral triangle has three sides of 12 cm each. What is its perimeter in cm?
activities.explanation: The perimeter is 3 * 12 = 36 cm.

activities.prompt: One round on Akshi’s outer track covers 220 m. How far does he run in 2 rounds, in m?
activities.explanation: The total distance is 220 * 2 = 440 m.

activities.prompt: Akshi’s outer track covers 220 m in one round. He runs a distance of 1100 m. How many complete rounds does he run?
activities.explanation: The number of rounds is 1100 / 220 = 5 rounds.

activities.prompt: Put these distances from smallest to largest.
activities.explanation: Your order starts with 180 m and ends with 1260 m. Nicely sorted!

activities.explanation: 1100 ÷ 5 = 220 m. You worked it out correctly!

activities.prompt: Toshi covers 1260 m in 4 rounds. How long is one round of his inner track in m?
activities.explanation: The length of one round is 1260 / 4 = 315 m.

lessons.title: Understanding area

activities.prompt: How can you discover how much space different shapes cover?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Space, Squares and Shapes
activities.body:
You begin beside a carpet, wondering how much floor it covers. The floor has an area of 20 square metres. The square carpet has an area of 9 square metres.

You look at the part of the floor without carpet. Its area is 11 square metres. You compare the two areas.

Next, you tour a piece of land with an area of 120 square metres. Four square flower beds each have an area of 16 square metres.

Together, the four beds have an area of 64 square metres. The remaining land has an area of 56 square metres. You break regions into unit squares to find areas. You also use rectangles and triangles, whose areas can be calculated.

Finally, you compare two closed figures. They can have the same area but different perimeters. They can also have the same perimeter but different areas.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What area tells us
activities.body: Area tells us how much surface a shape covers. In the carpet example, the floor has 20 square metres. The square carpet has 9 square metres, so 11 square metres remain uncovered. The land has 120 square metres. Its four flower beds cover 64 square metres, leaving 56 square metres. We can find areas by unit squares, rectangles and triangles. Figures may share area or perimeter without sharing both.
keyPoints: The uncovered floor has an area of 11 square metres.
The remaining land has an area of 56 square metres.
Different closed figures can share area or perimeter.
activities.explanation: Area measures the surface a shape covers.

tasks.then: Different shapes can cover the same area.

activities.explanation: Area counts how many unit squares cover a shape.

activities.explanation: Area of a square = side x side = 4 x 4 = 16 square metres.

activities.explanation: Remaining area = complete land - four flower beds = 100 - 4 x 10 = 60 square metres.

lessons.title: Estimating area with squares

activities.prompt: Can squares on your paper reveal a shape’s hidden area?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Area Squares
activities.body:
You place a simple closed shape on squared paper. You count the squares inside it. You take each square’s area as one square unit. Together, these counts estimate the shape’s area.

Some squares are only partly inside. You ignore portions smaller than half a square. You count a square when more than half is inside. You count it too when exactly half is inside.

Now you try circles as measuring units. Circles cannot be packed tightly without gaps between them. These gaps make accurate area measurement difficult. So circles are not the best choice.

You also look at other shapes. Triangles and rectangles can fill a space without overlaps and gaps. Squares are the best shapes for measuring area. You use them to estimate area on the squared paper.

Finally, you return to your shape. You check every square along the boundary. You apply the half-square rule each time. Then you report your estimate in square units.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Counting squares for area
activities.body: Use squared paper or graph paper to estimate a simple closed shape's area. Each square's area is one square unit. Ignore portions smaller than half a square. Count a square when more than half is inside. Also count a square when exactly half is inside.
keyPoints: Use squared paper or graph paper.
Each square's area is one square unit.
Ignore portions smaller than half a square.
Count squares with more than half inside.
Count squares with exactly half inside.
activities.explanation: These rules show which squares count towards the area.

activities.prompt: What can you use to estimate the area of a simple closed shape?

activities.explanation: Each of the 3 rows has 2 squares. So the estimated area is 3 × 2 square units.

activities.explanation: The triangles fill the rectangle without gaps or overlaps, so each triangle has area 60 ÷ 3 square cm.

activities.explanation: Squares are good units to measure area. The area by squares is 12 square units.

lessons.title: Area of a triangle

activities.prompt: What will you discover when a rectangle meets a diagonal?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Triangle Area Tour
activities.body:
You meet a rectangle called ABCD. Its diagonal gives you a cut. When you cut along that diagonal, the rectangle becomes two triangles. You can now compare their areas.

You place the red triangle and blue triangle together. They can overlap each other exactly. Because their areas match, neither one takes more space than the other. You see the same area in two matching shapes.

Now you look at triangle BAD. It has half the area of rectangle ABCD. The diagonal has helped you find this half. One triangle holds one half of the whole rectangle’s area.

Next, you meet triangle ABE. It is divided into triangles AEF and BEF. You follow the two smaller regions inside it. The names AEF and BEF show the two parts.

Finally, you compare triangle ABE with rectangles AFED and BFEC. Its area is half the sum of their areas. You also compare it with rectangle ABCD. Triangle ABE has half the area of rectangle ABCD. The tour ends with equal halves and exact matches.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Triangles from a rectangle
activities.body: A diagonal is the line used to cut a rectangle into two triangles. The two triangles can overlap each other exactly. The red and blue triangles have the same area. Triangle BAD has half the area of rectangle ABCD. Triangle ABE is divided into triangles AEF and BEF. Its area is half the sum of the areas of rectangles AFED and BFEC. Triangle ABE also has half the area of rectangle ABCD.
keyPoints: A diagonal cut produces two triangles.
The red and blue triangles have the same area.
Triangle ABE splits into AEF and BEF, and has half the area of ABCD.
activities.explanation: These facts show how triangles can have half the area of a rectangle.

pairs: Cutting a rectangle along its diagonal

activities.explanation: Each pair matches the fact about that shape.

activities.explanation: Cutting along the diagonal produces two triangles.

activities.explanation: Triangle BAD has half the area of rectangle ABCD, so its area is a/2 square cm.

activities.prompt: Rectangle ABCD is 7 cm long and 4 cm wide. Triangle BAD has half the area of the rectangle. What is the area of triangle BAD in square cm?
activities.explanation: First find the rectangle's area as l*w. Triangle BAD has half that area, so its area is (l*w)/2 square cm.

activities.explanation: The two smaller triangles make triangle ABE, so their areas are added: x+y square cm.

activities.explanation: Triangle ABE has half the area of rectangle ABCD, so its area is a/2 square cm.

lessons.title: Comparing areas and perimeters

activities.prompt: Can two equal areas have different perimeters?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Areas and Perimeters
activities.body:
You begin with two figures. Each uses nine unit squares. The first has a perimeter of 12 units. The second has a perimeter of 20 units. So, equal areas can have different perimeters.

The smallest possible perimeter for the nine unit squares is 12 cm. The largest possible perimeter is 20 cm. You can now compare both shapes without measuring every edge.

Next, you visit Charan’s house. Its area is 1050 square feet. Sharan’s house has an equal area. However, their perimeters differ. Charan’s perimeter is 130 feet. Sharan’s perimeter is 134 feet. Sharan’s house therefore has the greater perimeter.

You then inspect a rectangular garden. Its area is 300 square metres. Its length is 25 metres. You calculate that its width is 12 metres. The same area can help you find a missing dimension.

Finally, you look at a floor measuring 5 m by 4 m. Its uncarpeted part covers 11 square metres. Elsewhere, the area available for a lawn is 172 square metres. You finish by comparing where area and perimeter matter.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Area and perimeter
activities.body: Area is the amount of space inside a shape. Perimeter is the distance around its outside. Figures can have the same area but different perimeters. Nine unit squares show this. One figure has a perimeter of 12 units. Another has a perimeter of 20 units. Charan’s and Sharan’s houses also have equal areas but different perimeters.
keyPoints: Area compares the space inside a shape.
Perimeter compares the distance around the outside.
Equal areas can have different perimeters.
activities.explanation: Equal areas do not need equal perimeters.

activities.title: Same area, different perimeter

tasks.then: Area 12, perimeter 14.
Still area 12, but now perimeter 16.
Still area 12, but perimeter 26. Same area does not mean same perimeter.

activities.takeaway: Area and perimeter measure different things.
activities.explanation: Area and perimeter measure different things.

activities.explanation: This is the perimeter given for one nine-square figure.

activities.prompt: A rectangular art room is 8 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its perimeter in cm?
activities.explanation: Formula: 2 * (l + w). Using l = 8 and w = 4, the perimeter is 24 cm.

activities.prompt: Two tile designs use nine square tiles each. Their perimeters are 12 units and 18 units. By how many units is the second perimeter greater?
activities.explanation: Formula: q - p. Using p = 12 and q = 18, the second perimeter is 6 units greater.

activities.prompt: Charan's house has an area of 900 square feet. Sharan's house has the same area. What is the area of Sharan's house in square feet?
activities.explanation: Formula: a. Using a = 900, Sharan's house has an area of 900 square feet.

activities.prompt: Charan’s house and Sharan’s house have equal areas. Their perimeters are equal.
activities.explanation: Charan’s perimeter is 130 feet. Sharan’s is 134 feet, so they differ.

activities.prompt: A floor is 5 m by 4 m. The uncarpeted part has an area of 4 square metres. What is the carpeted area in square metres?
activities.explanation: Formula: 5 * 4 - u. Using u = 4, the carpeted area is 16 square metres.

activities.prompt: A garden is a rectangle. Its area is 300 square metres. Its length is 25 metres. What is its width in metres?
activities.explanation: Formula: a / 25. Using a = 300, the width is 12 metres.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: fractions and equal shares; fractional units and measuring lengths; marking fractions on a number line; mixed fractions.

lessons.title: Fractions and Equal Shares

activities.prompt: How can sharing make every part equal?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sharing a Roti
activities.body:
Imagine you have one roti and two children. You share it equally between them. Each child receives half a roti.

You might meet one half written as one upon two. Fractions show how much each equal share is. You see this whenever a whole is shared equally.

Next, four children share the same roti. You make four equal parts. Each child gets one quarter. With five children, each gets one fifth. With nine children, each gets one ninth.

More children sharing the same roti means each child gets a smaller share. You see that sharing with more people gives each person less.

You learn that each part made from one unit is a fractional unit. This is another name for a unit fraction. Fractions have been used and named in India since ancient times. In the Rig Veda, three quarters was called tri-pada.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Sharing a Roti Equally
activities.body: Imagine one whole roti. If it is shared equally, each child receives the same fraction. Two children each receive one half. Four children each receive one quarter. More children means smaller shares. When one unit is divided into equal parts, each part is a fractional unit. Fractional units are also called unit fractions.
keyPoints: Fractions show equal shares of a whole.
More children receive smaller shares.
Fractional units are also called unit fractions.
activities.explanation: Equal shares make fractions, and smaller groups get bigger shares.

activities.title: Share a bar

tasks.say: Cut the bar into 8 equal parts.
tasks.then: More parts means each part is smaller.
4 out of 8 equal parts is one half.

activities.takeaway: A fraction counts equal parts of a whole.
activities.explanation: A fraction counts equal parts of a whole.

activities.prompt: One half is read as one upon two. If two children share 4 rotis equally, how much does each child get?

lessons.title: Fractional Units and Measuring Lengths

activities.prompt: How can folded paper help us measure lengths?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Fold and a Fraction
activities.body:
You begin with a paper strip and treat the whole strip as one unit long. Fold it once into two equal parts, and you create two half-unit parts. Fold the folded strip again, and it gives four equal parts.

Now imagine a chikki on your tour. Break it into three equal pieces, and each one is a one-third piece. A bigger piece of chikki contains three one-quarter pieces. You can divide a whole chikki into six equal parts. These equal parts can have different shapes.

Next, you meet fractional quantities, which can be measured using fractional units. You can describe a quantity by collecting fractional units together. You collect the fractional units to describe the quantity you measured.

Finally, you write a fraction such as three quarters. You read it as three quarters or three upon four. The top number is the numerator, and the bottom number is the denominator.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Using Fractional Units
activities.body: Imagine a whole chikki. A paper strip can be one unit long. Fold it into two equal parts, then fold once more. You now have four equal parts. These parts help measure fractional quantities using fractional units. Collect fractional units to describe a quantity. In a fraction, the top number is the numerator. The bottom number is the denominator.
keyPoints: A paper strip can be treated as one unit long.
Folding it twice makes four equal parts.
The top number is the numerator and the bottom number is the denominator.
activities.explanation: These facts connect equal folds, fractional units and fraction names.

activities.title: Reading Fraction Parts
activities.body: Fractions help us name fractional units. The fraction three quarters can be read as three quarters or three upon four. Its top number is the numerator. Its bottom number is the denominator. Six equal parts of a whole chikki can make pieces with different shapes. Equal parts can therefore have different shapes.
keyPoints: Three quarters can also be read as three upon four.
The numerator is the top number.
Equal parts of a whole can have different shapes.
activities.explanation: These words help us read fractions and describe equal parts.

activities.title: Equal Folds
activities.prompt: If you fold a paper strip into two equal parts, you get two half-unit parts.
activities.explanation: The two equal parts are each half of the whole strip.

activities.title: One Third of Chikki
activities.prompt: A chikki broken into ______ equal pieces has a one-third piece.
activities.hint: Think about how many equal pieces make one-third pieces.
activities.explanation: Breaking a chikki into three equal pieces makes one-third pieces.

activities.title: Match Parts and Facts
activities.prompt: Match each description to its matching fact.
pairs: a chikki broken into three equal pieces
strip folded into two equal parts
activities.explanation: Each description matches the equal parts or pieces in the lesson.

activities.title: Fold and Describe
activities.prompt: Put the folding steps in order, then describe the quantity.
items: Treat the paper strip as one unit long.
Fold it into two equal parts.
Collect fractional units to describe a quantity.
activities.explanation: Two equal folds create four equal parts for measuring a fractional quantity.

activities.prompt: A paper strip is treated as one unit long. If 4 paper strips are placed end to end, how many units long is the joined strip?
activities.explanation: Each strip is 1 unit long, so the joined length is n*1 = 4 units.

activities.prompt: A paper strip is folded into two equal parts, making two half-unit parts. If 3 paper strips are folded this way, how many half-unit parts are made?
activities.explanation: Each strip makes 2 half-unit parts, so the total is n*2 = 6 half-unit parts.

activities.prompt: A paper strip is folded in half twice, making four equal parts. If 5 paper strips are folded this way, how many quarter-unit parts are made?
activities.explanation: Each strip makes 4 quarter-unit parts, so the total is n*4 = 20 quarter-unit parts.

activities.prompt: A chikki broken into three equal pieces has a one-third piece. If 9 one-third pieces are collected, how many whole chikkis do they make?
activities.explanation: Three one-third pieces make one whole chikki, so n/3 = 3 whole chikkis.

activities.prompt: The bigger piece of chikki contains three one-quarter pieces. If there are 3 one-quarter pieces, how many bigger pieces can be made?
activities.explanation: Each bigger piece needs 3 one-quarter pieces, so q/3 = 1 bigger pieces.

activities.prompt: Six equal parts of a whole chikki can make pieces with different shapes. If 3 whole chikkis are each broken into six equal pieces, how many one-sixth pieces are made?
activities.explanation: Each chikki makes 6 one-sixth pieces, so n*6 = 18 one-sixth pieces.

lessons.title: Marking Fractions on a Number Line

activities.prompt: How can you show fractions on a number line?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Fractions on a Number Line
activities.body:
Imagine you meet a number line that can show lengths equal to whole units. You can also use it to mark lengths equal to fractions.

Start by looking from 0 to 1. This distance is one unit long. You split it into two equal parts. Each part is one half.

In the first example, the blue line is one half unit long. You mark that point carefully. This helps you see where one half belongs.

Now explore other divisions. You can divide one unit into three equal parts. You can also divide it into five equal parts. Each equal part marks another fraction.

What happens with finer sharing? You can divide one unit into eight equal parts. Between 0 and 1, there are uncountably many fractions. The number line keeps offering more places to explore.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Fractions on a Number Line
activities.body: A number line shows lengths from 0 to 1. The gap between them is one whole unit. You can divide this gap into equal parts. Two equal parts make halves. You can also divide one unit into three, five or eight equal parts. Marking these parts helps you place fractions between 0 and 1.
keyPoints: The distance from 0 to 1 is one whole unit.
One unit can be divided into equal parts.
Equal parts show fraction lengths.
activities.explanation: This helps you see how fractions fit between 0 and 1.

activities.title: Many Fraction Lengths
activities.body: One unit can also be divided into three, five or eight equal parts. Each marked part shows a fraction length. There are uncountably many fractions between 0 and 1. This means countless different fraction lengths fit between those points on the same number line.
keyPoints: Equal parts can show different fraction lengths.
Many fraction lengths fit between 0 and 1.
The number line can mark fraction lengths.
activities.explanation: You can now connect equal parts with the many fractions between 0 and 1.

activities.prompt: The distance between 0 and 1 is one unit long.
activities.explanation: Yes! The distance from 0 to 1 represents one whole unit.

activities.prompt: The line from 0 to 1 is cut into two equal parts. Each part is one ______.
activities.hint: This is one of two equal parts.
activities.explanation: Cutting the line into two equal parts makes each part one half.

activities.prompt: Match each division to its matching fact.
pairs: The blue line is one half unit long
One unit can be divided into three equal parts
One unit can be divided into five equal parts
One unit can be divided into eight equal parts
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each division uses equal parts, and the blue line shows one half unit.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to mark one half.
items: Start with the distance from 0 to 1
Divide it into two equal parts
activities.explanation: You have it! Dividing the distance equally gives two halves. Marking one part shows one half.

activities.prompt: A number line starts at 0. A bus moves 3 whole units to the right. How many whole units from 0 is the bus?
activities.explanation: The bus moves 3 whole units, so it is 3 whole units from 0.

activities.prompt: A blue line from 0 to 8 cm is divided into 2 equal parts. How long is one part in cm?
activities.explanation: Each equal part is 8 / 2 cm = 4 cm.

activities.prompt: A line from 0 to 15 cm is divided into 3 equal parts. How long is one part in cm?
activities.explanation: Each equal part is 15 / 3 cm = 5 cm.

activities.prompt: A ribbon from 0 to 25 cm is divided into 5 equal parts. How long is one part in cm?
activities.explanation: Each equal part is 25 / 5 cm = 5 cm.

activities.prompt: A line from 0 to 16 cm is divided into 8 equal parts. How long is one part in cm?
activities.explanation: Each equal part is 16 / 8 cm = 2 cm.

activities.prompt: One unit on a number line is divided into 3 equal parts. How many equal parts are there in one unit?
activities.explanation: The one unit is divided into 3 equal parts, so the answer is 3.

lessons.title: Mixed Fractions

activities.prompt: How do you compare a fraction with one whole?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Mixed Numbers
activities.body:
Imagine meeting fractions during this tour. You may wonder how each compares with one whole unit. If the numerator is smaller than the denominator, the fraction is smaller than one unit. If the numerator is larger than the denominator, the fraction is greater than one unit.

You try three halves, five halves and seven halves. All three are greater than one unit. Now look again at three halves. It equals one whole unit plus one half. Next, you meet four thirds. This fraction is also greater than one unit. Some fractions greater than one cannot be written as mixed numbers.

You now discover a mixed number. It contains a whole-number part. The fraction smaller than one in it is called the fractional part. You next meet eight thirds. It is also called two and two thirds.

Before you finish, write a mixed number as a regular fraction. You can check each fraction by comparing its numerator with its denominator. Smaller numerators show fractions smaller than one unit. Larger numerators show fractions greater than one unit.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Understanding Mixed Fractions
activities.body: A fraction smaller than one unit has a numerator smaller than its denominator. A fraction greater than one unit has a numerator larger than its denominator. Three halves, five halves and seven halves are greater than one unit. A mixed number contains a whole-number part and a fractional part. The fractional part is the fraction smaller than one. Eight thirds is also called two and two thirds.
keyPoints: Compare the numerator and denominator with the denominator.
A mixed number has a whole-number part and a fractional part.
Eight thirds is also called two and two thirds.
activities.explanation: These facts help you recognise and name mixed numbers.

activities.title: More than one whole

tasks.say: Use 4 parts in each bar and shade 4.
tasks.then: 4/4 is exactly one whole.
7/4 is one whole and three quarters.

activities.takeaway: A mixed fraction is wholes and a part.
activities.explanation: A mixed fraction is wholes and a part.

activities.title: Reading a Mixed Number
activities.body: Eight thirds is also called two and two thirds. This mixed number has a whole-number part of two. Its fractional part is two thirds. A mixed number can be written as one regular fraction. Some fractions greater than one cannot be written as mixed numbers.
keyPoints: A mixed number contains a whole-number part and a fractional part.
A mixed number can be written as a regular fraction.
Not every fraction greater than one can become a mixed number.
activities.explanation: You can identify the two parts of a mixed number.

activities.prompt: Which fraction equals one whole unit plus one half?
options: Three halves
One half
Four thirds
Eight thirds
activities.explanation: Three halves equal one whole unit plus one half.

activities.prompt: Match each part with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a fraction with the rule from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Five halves is smaller than one unit.
activities.explanation: Five halves is greater than one unit.

activities.prompt: A bus is filled to 6/3 of its capacity. How many thirds of a bus are there beyond one full bus?
activities.explanation: Four thirds is already greater than one bus because 4 is greater than 3. In general, subtract 3 thirds from n thirds.

activities.prompt: A ribbon is 5 and 1/5 cm long. What is the whole-number part of its length in cm?
activities.explanation: The whole-number part of the mixed number is w.

activities.prompt: A ribbon is 1 and 1/7 cm long. What is the fractional part of its length in cm?
activities.explanation: The fractional part is the fraction smaller than one, which is n/d.

activities.prompt: What is true about some fractions greater than one unit?
options: All can be written as mixed numbers.
Some cannot be written as mixed numbers.
All contain only a fractional part.
They all equal one whole unit.
activities.explanation: Some fractions greater than one cannot be written as mixed numbers.

activities.prompt: Three amounts are 9/2, 3/2, and 9/2 of a bus. How many half-bus loads are left after taking one bus from each amount?
activities.explanation: Each amount is greater than one bus. One bus equals two half-bus loads, so subtract 2 from each numerator and add the remainders.

activities.prompt: The fraction 8/3 is also called 2 and 2/3. A ribbon is 3 and 1/9 cm long. What is its length as a regular fraction in cm?
activities.explanation: For 8/3, multiply the whole part by the denominator and add the numerator: 2 x 3 + 2 gives 8. In general, (w x d + n)/d gives the regular fraction.

lessons.title: Equivalent Fractions and Lowest Terms

activities.prompt: Could two different fractions show the same amount?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Equivalent Fractions and Lowest Terms
activities.body:
Imagine two strips of equal length. One is split in half. The other is split into quarters. You hold one half and two quarters. Do they cover the same length?

They cover the same length. Different fractional units can show equal shares. Fractions with equal shares are called equivalent fractions. Three sixths also match one half. So, one half, two quarters and three sixths are equivalent.

Now picture sharing units among children. When the same units are shared among more children, each child’s share is less. When the same number of children share more units, each child gets a larger share.

Sometimes an equivalent fraction is not in its simplest form. Six ninths has the simpler form two thirds. In lowest terms, a fraction’s numerator and denominator have no common factor except 1. In lowest terms, they are as small as possible.

To find lowest terms, divide the numerator and denominator by their highest common factor. You can also multiply both by the same number and keep equivalent fractions equal. For example, thirty-six sixtieths becomes three fifths in lowest terms.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Equal shares and simpler fractions
activities.body: Equivalent fractions show equal shares even when they use different fractional units. One half, two quarters, and three sixths are equivalent. A fraction has a numerator and denominator. Lowest terms means they have no common factor except 1 and are as small as possible. Divide both by their highest common factor to find this form.
keyPoints: Equivalent fractions show equal shares.
One half, two quarters, and three sixths are equivalent.
Divide both parts by their highest common factor.
activities.explanation: Dividing both parts by their highest common factor makes a fraction simpler.

activities.title: Find equal fractions

tasks.say: Make the same amount using 6 parts.
tasks.then: 3/6 is also 0.5: the same amount with smaller pieces.
5/10 is equal to 1/2 too.

activities.takeaway: Equivalent fractions name the same amount.
activities.explanation: Equivalent fractions name the same amount.

activities.prompt: Equivalent fractions can show the same length with different fractional units.
activities.explanation: Different fractional units can show the same length.

activities.prompt: When is a fraction in lowest terms?
options: When the top and bottom numbers are equal
When top and bottom share no factor except 1
When it has the biggest numbers possible
When the top number is bigger than the bottom
activities.explanation: Lowest terms means the only common factor is 1. A factor is a number that divides another number exactly.

activities.title: Match the equivalent fractions
activities.prompt: Match each fraction with its equivalent form.
activities.explanation: Each matched pair shows equal shares using different fractions.

activities.prompt: A fraction is in lowest terms when its numerator and denominator have no common factor except ______.
activities.hint: This is the smallest number and the only allowed common factor.
activities.explanation: The only common factor allowed in lowest terms is 1.

activities.prompt: A rope is 36 cm long. It is measured in units of 4 cm each. How many units are needed?
activities.explanation: The number of units is the length divided by the size of one unit: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 units.

activities.prompt: 2/36 of a marble is the same as 3/x of a marble. What is the denominator x (the bottom number)?
activities.explanation: Equal fractions have the same value. So 2/36 = 3/x. Then x = (36 × 3) ÷ 2 = 54.

activities.prompt: The fraction 3/4 becomes an equal fraction when you multiply the top and bottom by 2. How many equal parts are in the new denominator?
activities.explanation: Multiply the bottom number by 2: 4 × 2 = 8 equal parts.

activities.prompt: A fraction has numerator 5 and denominator 13. If it is in lowest terms, what is the only common factor of its numerator and denominator?
activities.explanation: A fraction is in lowest terms when its numerator and denominator have no common factor except 1.

activities.prompt: A fraction has numerator 3 × 3 and denominator 13 × 3. The numbers 3 and 13 have no common factor. What is the highest common factor of the numerator and denominator?
activities.explanation: Remove the common factor 3. Then 3 and 13 have no common factor. So the highest common factor is 3.

activities.prompt: A bar is divided into 3*4 equal parts, and 11*4 parts are shaded. Divide both numbers by their highest common factor. How many shaded parts are in the lowest-terms numerator?
activities.explanation: Dividing the shaded parts by the highest common factor gives (11 × 4) ÷ 4 = 11. For example, 36/60 becomes 3/5.

lessons.title: Comparing, Adding and Subtracting Fractions

activities.prompt: How can you compare and combine fractional pieces fairly?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Fractional Journey
activities.body:
Imagine meeting fractional pieces on a maths journey. Which is larger? How can you join or break them apart?

First, change the fractions to equivalent fractions with the same denominator. Then compare their numerators. Forty-five is a common multiple of five and nine. You can use it as a shared denominator.

Now suppose you add fractions with the same fractional unit. You add their fractional units. If the fractional units differ, first change them to equivalent fractions with the same denominator. Then add the numerators and keep the denominator. Write the result in lowest terms when needed.

Subtraction follows a similar path. First, change fractions to equivalent fractions with the same fractional unit. Then subtract the numerators and keep the same denominator.

Words from India give us a glimpse of fractions. In Sanskrit, a fraction was called bhinna, meaning broken. Bhaga and an sha were names for a part or piece. General fractions and their arithmetic rules were first introduced in India.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: A Helpful Fraction Plan
activities.body: To compare fractions, first change them to equivalent fractions with the same denominator. Then compare their numerators. To add fractions, make their fractional units the same. Add the numerators and keep the denominator. To subtract fractions, use the same denominator, then subtract the numerators. Write the result in lowest terms when needed. In Sanskrit, a fraction was called bhinna, meaning broken. Bhaga and an sha meant a part or piece.
keyPoints: Compare fractions using equivalent fractions with the same denominator.
Add and subtract the numerators after making fractional units match.
Bhaga and an sha meant a part or piece.
activities.explanation: These steps help you compare, add and subtract fractions carefully.

activities.title: Which Fraction Is Greater?
activities.prompt: Which fraction is greater: 9/5 or 5/9?
options: They are equal
You cannot tell
activities.explanation: With denominator 45, compare numerators 81 and 25. Since 81 is greater, 9/5 is greater.

activities.prompt: After fractions have the same denominator, compare their numerators.
activities.explanation: The fractions now have one denominator, so compare their numerators.

activities.title: Match the Fraction Job
activities.prompt: Match each fraction job with the correct step.
pairs: Make the fractional units the same
Add numerators and keep the denominator
Subtract numerators and keep the same denominator
activities.explanation: Matching fractional units comes first. Then compare, add or subtract the numerators.

activities.title: Order the Addition Steps
activities.prompt: Put the addition steps in the correct order.
items: Change to equivalent fractions with the same denominator
Write the result in lowest terms if needed
activities.explanation: Make the fractional units equal before adding the numerators.

activities.prompt: A blue tray is 6/5 full of marbles. A red tray is 3/5 full. How many fifths fuller is the blue tray?
activities.explanation: The denominators are already the same, so compare the numerators. The blue tray is fuller by (6-3)/5 fifths of a tray.

activities.prompt: One heap has 2/5 of a bag of marbles. Another heap has 4/5 of a bag. How many bags of marbles do they make in all?
activities.explanation: The fractional unit is the same. Add the numerators and keep the denominator. The total is (2+4)/5 bags of marbles.

activities.prompt: A baker has 4/5 of a bag of flour. How many forty-fifths of a bag of flour is this?
activities.explanation: Since 45 is a common multiple of 5 and 9, change 4/5 to 4*9/45. Thus the amount is 4*9 forty-fifths of a bag of flour.

activities.prompt: A cart has 3/5 of a bag of rice. It also has 2/9 of another bag of rice. How many forty-fifths of a bag do you have in all?
activities.explanation: Change 3/5 to 3*9/45 and 2/9 to 2*5/45. Add the numerators and keep 45, giving (3*9+2*5)/45 forty-fifths of a bag of rice.

activities.prompt: A shop has 15/5 of a bag of laddoos. It also has 27/9 of another bag. How many whole bags (no bits left over) do you have in all?
activities.explanation: Change both fractional units to forty-fifths, add the numerators and keep 45. The numerator is a multiple of 45, so (15*9+27*5)/45 gives a whole number of bags in lowest terms.

activities.prompt: A blue heap has 7/5 of a bag of sand. A red heap has 2/9 of a bag of sand. The blue heap is bigger by how many forty-fifths of a bag?
activities.explanation: Change 7/5 to 7*9/45 and 2/9 to 2*5/45. Compare the new numerators and subtract them, giving (7*9-2*5)/45 forty-fifths of a bag.

chapters.title: Playing with Constructions
chapters.summary: In this chapter: artwork with a compass; squares and rectangles; constructing squares and rectangles; exploring rectangles.

lessons.title: Artwork with a Compass

activities.prompt: What wonders can your compass uncover on a page?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your Compass Adventure
activities.body:
You open a book of artwork. It includes straight lines, circles, and other figures among curves. Your compass feels like a tiny guide. Soon, you meet a point called P.

From P, mark as many points as possible in different directions. Each point is 4 cm from P. All such points form a circle. P is called the centre.

The compass tip and pencil point must be 4 cm apart. Keep the compass point fixed and move only the pencil. The curve it makes is a circle. The distance from the centre to any point on the circle is the radius.

The chapter asks whether using instruments makes construction easier. You can explore this while drawing. The length of the central line is not specified. So, focus on your compass.

In Wavy Wave, you begin with a surprise. The first wave is drawn as a half circle. Hold the compass steady and let the pencil travel. Soon, straight edges and flowing curves share your page.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How a Compass Makes a Circle
activities.body: Lines and curves appear in the book. A compass helps draw a circle when its points are 4 cm apart. Keep the compass point fixed and move only the pencil. Every point on the new circle lies 4 cm from P. P is the centre. The radius is the distance from the centre to any point on the circle. The chapter asks whether instruments make construction easier.
keyPoints: Keep the compass point fixed and move only the pencil.
Every point on the circle is 4 cm from P.
P is the centre, and the radius reaches from P to the circle.
activities.explanation: Keeping the compass point fixed helps every circle point stay the same distance from P.

activities.title: The Compass Shape
activities.prompt: Which shape does the curve made by a compass make?
options: A straight line
A circle
A half circle
A central line
activities.explanation: The curve made by the compass is a circle.

activities.title: Points Around P
activities.prompt: Why do all marked points 4 cm from P fit one circle?
options: They all have the same distance from P.
They all lie on one straight line.
They all have different distances from P.
Their central line has a fixed length.
activities.explanation: All these points are 4 cm from P, so they form one circle.

activities.title: Circle Words
activities.prompt: Match each word or phrase with its correct partner.
pairs: distance from the centre to the circle
activities.explanation: P is the centre, while the radius reaches from the centre to the circle.

activities.title: Draw a Circle
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Set the compass tip and pencil 4 cm apart.
activities.explanation: Set the gap, hold one point, move the pencil, and watch the circle appear.

activities.prompt: A circle has centre P. Point Q is on the circle and Q is 5 cm from P. What is the radius of the circle in cm?
activities.explanation: The radius is the distance from the centre P to Q, so r = 5 cm.

activities.prompt: A child puts the compass tip on P. The pencil point is 2 cm away from P. How far is the pencil point from P, in cm?
activities.explanation: The distance from P to the pencil point is r = 2 cm.

activities.prompt: A compass draws a circle of radius 2 cm with centre P. How far apart must the compass tip and pencil point be in cm?
activities.explanation: The compass opening must equal the radius, so the distance is r = 2 cm.

activities.prompt: The full circle for the first wave in Wavy Wave has radius 2 cm. The wave is drawn using a half circle. What radius is used for the half circle in cm?
activities.explanation: The half circle uses the same circle radius, so r = 2 cm.

activities.prompt: A child marks 5 points. Each point is 4 cm from P. The points go in different directions. How many points are marked?
activities.explanation: The number of marked points is n = 5 points.

lessons.title: Squares and Rectangles

activities.prompt: What happens when you turn a square around?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Shape Tour
activities.body:
You begin with two familiar shapes. Each has straight sides.

First, you meet a rectangle. Its corners are A, B, C and D. The sides travel around it as AB, BC, CD and DA. The angles at its corners are ∠A, ∠B, ∠C and ∠D. Each one measures 90°.

Notice that AD and BC make another pair of opposite sides. These sides have equal lengths. Now, you turn the rectangle. It remains a rectangle.

Next, you find a square. All its sides have equal lengths. Its angles still measure 90°. Turn it carefully. Its side lengths and angles do not change. Even when the square is turned, each angle remains 90°.

Finally, you learn a naming trick. A valid name travels around the rectangle. You can start at any corner. Then follow the sides in order. Try A, B, C, D, A, or begin somewhere else.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Squares and Rectangles
activities.body: A rectangle has straight sides. Its corners are A, B, C and D. Its sides are AB, BC, CD and DA. The opposite sides, AB with CD and AD with BC, have equal lengths. Every angle measures 90°. A square has equal sides and 90° angles. Rotating a square does not change its side lengths or angles.
keyPoints: A rectangle has opposite sides of equal lengths.
Every rectangle angle measures 90°.
A square has equal sides and 90° angles.
activities.explanation: These properties help you recognise and describe squares and rectangles.

activities.title: Equal Sides and Rotation
activities.body: Opposite sides of a rectangle have equal lengths. AB and CD form one pair. AD and BC form the other pair. Every rectangle angle measures 90°. A square also has equal sides. Rotating a square does not change its side lengths or angles. A rotated rectangle is still a rectangle.
keyPoints: Opposite rectangle sides have equal lengths.
All rectangle angles measure 90°.
Rotation does not change a square's side lengths or angles.
activities.explanation: Equal sides and right angles help you identify these shapes.

activities.prompt: All the angles of the rectangle are 90°.
activities.explanation: Yes! Every angle of a rectangle measures 90°.

activities.prompt: Which group lists all four sides of the rectangle?
options: AB, BC, CD and DA
AB, BC, AC and DA
AB, CD, AD and AC
AB, BC, CD and DB
activities.explanation: The rectangle's sides are AB, BC, CD and DA.

activities.prompt: After rotating a square, its angles are no longer 90°.
activities.explanation: The rotation keeps every angle of the square at 90°.

activities.prompt: A rectangle is 15 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its perimeter in cm?
activities.explanation: The perimeter is 2 * (15 + 4) = 38 cm.

activities.prompt: A square has sides of 3 cm each. What is its perimeter in cm?
activities.explanation: The perimeter of the square is 4 * 3 = 12 cm.

activities.prompt: The perimeter of a square is 16 cm. What is the length of one side in cm?
activities.explanation: One side is 16 / 4 = 4 cm.

activities.prompt: A rectangle is rotated. A child measures angle A as 120 degrees. What is the correct measure of angle A in degrees?
activities.explanation: A rotated rectangle is still a rectangle, so every angle measures 90 degrees.

activities.prompt: Match each valid name to its starting corner.
activities.explanation: Each name starts at a corner and travels around the rectangle.

activities.prompt: A square has sides of 4 cm. It is rotated without changing its size. What is the length of one side after rotation in cm?
activities.explanation: Rotation does not change the side length, so one side is still 4 cm.

activities.prompt: A valid name for rectangle ABCD travels around the shape and may start at vertex 1. How many sides are included in the complete name?
activities.explanation: The name travels around all four sides: AB, BC, CD and DA.

lessons.title: Constructing Squares and Rectangles

activities.prompt: Can you discover how to build squares and rectangles?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Squares and Rectangles
activities.body:
First, you construct square PQRS, with each side measuring 6 cm. Draw a perpendicular to PQ through P. Mark point S on the perpendicular. Set PS at 6 cm using a ruler. You can also mark S using a compass.

Now draw a perpendicular to PQ through Q. Using the compass lets you mark the next point easily. With care, you build the square PQRS. Each side has the same length of 6 cm.

Next, you construct a rectangle with sides 4 cm and 6 cm. Draw its first side with your ruler. Use the compass to mark the next point. Check the finished rectangle against both rectangle properties.

You also construct a rectangle with sides 2 cm and 10 cm. Repeat the careful construction steps. Use the ruler to set the lengths. Then use the compass to mark each next point.

Finally, notice the chapter’s special question. It asks about a four-sided figure with all angles equal to 90º. Which properties will you check first?
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Building squares and rectangles
activities.body: To construct square PQRS, draw a perpendicular to PQ through P. Mark S on this perpendicular so PS measures 6 cm. Use a ruler to set the length, or use a compass. A perpendicular to PQ is also drawn through Q. The compass helps you mark the next point easily. Rectangles with sides 4 cm and 6 cm, or 2 cm and 10 cm, can also be built.
keyPoints: PS measures 6 cm.
Perpendiculars are drawn through P and Q.
Rectangles with different side lengths are constructed.
activities.explanation: Careful measuring and right angles help you make each shape.

activities.prompt: Point S is marked on the perpendicular to PQ.
activities.explanation: The construction marks S on the perpendicular through P.

activities.prompt: The length PS is ______ cm.
activities.hint: Use the ruler to measure PS.
activities.explanation: The square is constructed with side length 6 cm.

activities.prompt: Match each square detail with its construction step.
pairs: A perpendicular to PQ is drawn through it
It is marked on the perpendicular
The compass helps mark it easily
activities.explanation: Each detail matches the given steps for constructing square PQRS.

activities.prompt: Through which point is a perpendicular to PQ also drawn?
options: P
Q
R
S
activities.explanation: The second perpendicular to PQ is drawn through Q.

activities.prompt: A square PQRS has side 6 cm. What is the length of PS in cm?
activities.explanation: PS is one side of the square, so its length is s cm.

activities.prompt: A square PQRS has sides 5 cm long. How far, in cm, should the compass be set to mark S from P?
activities.explanation: The compass distance from P to S is the same as the side length, s cm.

activities.prompt: Square PQRS has a side PQ. A line goes through P. It is perpendicular to PQ (it makes a square corner). What is the angle between them in degrees?
activities.explanation: A perpendicular makes a right angle. So 90 + 0 × s = 90 degrees.

activities.prompt: A square PQRS has side 4 cm. How many of its sides are 4 cm long?
activities.explanation: All four sides of the square are equal, so (s/s)*4 = 4 sides.

activities.prompt: A rectangle is 10 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is the length in cm of each width side?
activities.explanation: The two opposite sides across the width of a rectangle each measure w cm.

lessons.sceneCaption: Use right angles and equal opposite sides to make and check squares and rectangles.

lessons.title: Exploring Rectangles

activities.prompt: Could two points hide a surprising distance?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Rectangle Tour
activities.body:
Imagine you begin inside a rectangle. Point X can move anywhere along the side AD. You may place X at either end point, A or D.

Point Y can be placed at either end point, B or C. You can find distance XY by measuring line XY. Now you can compare different placements.

When X and Y are equally placed, XY equals AB. Next, you choose placements that lie farthest apart. The farthest distance between X and Y equals AC or BD.

Now shift your attention to squares. You can divide the rectangle into two identical squares. All the shorter lines in that rectangle are equal.

You can also divide the rectangle into three identical squares. For three identical squares, the length is three times the breadth. Measure again, and explore every placement.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Points and distances in a rectangle
activities.body: Point X can move along AD. Point Y can be placed at B or C. Distance XY is found by measuring line XY. When X and Y are equally placed, XY equals AB. The farthest distance equals AC or BD. A rectangle can split into two identical squares. It can split into three identical squares. With three squares, length is three times breadth. Breadth means the shorter side.
keyPoints: X moves along AD; Y is placed at B or C.
Measure line XY to find its distance.
Three identical squares make length three times breadth.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you explore distances and square divisions in rectangles.

activities.prompt: Where can point X move?
options: Anywhere along AD
Only at B
Only at C
Outside the rectangle
activities.explanation: X is free to move anywhere along side AD.

activities.prompt: Point X can be placed at either end point A or D.
activities.explanation: Both A and D are end points of side AD.

activities.prompt: The distance XY is found by ______ the line XY.
activities.hint: Use the action given for finding a distance.
activities.explanation: You find the distance by measuring the line between the points.

activities.prompt: Which distance is the farthest between X and Y?
options: AB
AC or BD
AD
BC
activities.explanation: The greatest possible distance between X and Y equals AC or BD.

activities.prompt: X and Y are equally placed in rectangle ABCD. Side AB is 4 cm. What is the distance XY in cm?
activities.explanation: When X and Y are equally placed, XY = AB = 4 cm.

activities.prompt: The farthest distance between X and Y is diagonal AC. If AC is 5 cm, what is the distance XY in cm?
activities.explanation: At the farthest placement, XY = AC = 5 cm.

activities.prompt: A rectangle is divided into two identical squares. Its breadth is 3 cm. What is the length of each shorter side in cm?
activities.explanation: All shorter sides are equal, so each shorter side is 3 cm.

activities.prompt: A rectangle is divided into three identical squares. Its breadth is 3 cm. What is its length in cm?
activities.explanation: For b = 3 cm, 3*b = 3*3 = 9 cm.

lessons.title: Exploring Diagonals of Rectangles and Squares

activities.prompt: What do diagonals reveal about the corners of a rectangle?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Rectangle Diagonals
activities.body:
You begin with rectangle PQRS. The lines PR and QS are called the diagonals. You follow each one across the shape. You wonder how these crossing lines affect the corners.

At P and R, you find right angles. These are opposite angles. At Q and S, you find the other opposite pair. A diagonal divides each pair into smaller angles. The diagonal PR divides angle R into two smaller angles. It also divides angle P into the angles c and d.

When both diagonals meet, they form eight angles. You count them around the crossing point. Each diagonal splits the opposite corners into smaller angles. You compare the pairs as you trace them.

Your exploration also includes a rectangle with all four sides equal. When two adjacent sides are equal, the rectangle becomes a square. To find D, you draw a perpendicular to BC at C. A compass can mark D so that AD equals BC. Your tour ends with a square.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Meet the Diagonals
activities.body: In rectangle PQRS, the diagonals are PR and QS. These two lines are called the diagonals. The right angles at P and R are opposite angles. The right angles at Q and S are the other opposite pair. A diagonal divides each pair of opposite angles into smaller angles. The diagonal PR divides angle R into two smaller angles. It also divides angle P into angles c and d. The two diagonals form eight angles.
keyPoints: PR and QS are the diagonals.
P and R form one opposite pair.
Q and S form the other opposite pair.
The two diagonals form eight angles.
activities.explanation: Diagonals split opposite angles and create eight angles together.

activities.title: Find the Diagonals
activities.prompt: Which lines are the diagonals of rectangle PQRS?
options: PR and QS
PQ and RS
QR and SP
Only PR
activities.explanation: PR and QS are the two diagonals of rectangle PQRS.

activities.title: An Opposite Pair
activities.prompt: The right angles at P and R are opposite angles.
activities.explanation: P and R form one pair of opposite right angles.

activities.title: Name the Lines
activities.prompt: The lines PR and QS are called the ______.
activities.hint: These are special lines in rectangle PQRS.
activities.explanation: PR and QS are called the diagonals of the rectangle.

activities.title: Match the Facts
activities.prompt: Match each part with its fact.
activities.explanation: Each diagonal divides opposite angles into smaller angles.

activities.title: Follow Diagonal PR
activities.prompt: What does diagonal PR do to angle R?
options: It divides it into two smaller angles.
It leaves it unchanged.
It turns it into angle c and d.
It removes the right angle.
activities.explanation: Diagonal PR divides angle R into two smaller angles.

activities.title: Squares and Point D
activities.body: A rectangle can have all four sides equal. This is the square case in the exploration. When two adjacent sides are equal, the rectangle becomes a square. To find point D, draw a perpendicular to BC at C. A compass can mark D so that AD equals BC.
keyPoints: All four equal sides form the square case.
Two equal adjacent sides make a square.
A perpendicular to BC at C finds D.
AD can equal BC using a compass.
activities.explanation: Equal sides can create a square, while a compass helps mark D.

activities.title: Find Point D
activities.prompt: How is point D found in the given construction?
options: Draw a diagonal from A to C.
Draw a parallel through A.
Draw a circle centred at B.
Draw a perpendicular to BC at C.
activities.explanation: Drawing a perpendicular to BC at C is the stated way to find D.

activities.title: Choose the Correct Method
activities.prompt: Which statement uses the square and compass facts correctly?
options: Equal opposite sides make a square, and AB must equal CD.
Equal adjacent sides make a square, and a compass can mark D so AD equals BC.
All four equal sides leave a rectangle unchanged, and AD need not equal BC.
Equal adjacent sides leave a rectangle unchanged, and AD must be smaller than BC.
activities.explanation: Equal adjacent sides make a square, and the compass can make AD equal BC.

activities.prompt: A child draws diagonal PR in each of 2 rectangles. A diagonal goes from one corner to the opposite corner. How many small angles are at R in all?
activities.explanation: Diagonal PR splits the angle at R into 2 small angles. With a = 2, 2 × a = 2 × 2 = 4 small angles.

activities.prompt: Point D is found by drawing a perpendicular to BC at C in each of 2 rectangles. How many right angles at C are made altogether?
activities.explanation: Each perpendicular makes one right angle at C. For a = 2, a = 2 right angles.

lessons.title: Points Equidistant from Two Given Points

activities.prompt: How can circles help you find a point equally distant from two places?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Finding the Equidistant Point
activities.body:
Every border line of the house has length 5 cm. The task is to find point A, 5 cm from both B and C. Start by trying to find this point with a ruler. This method needs trial and error. You test possible points and check both distances.

Now you simplify the construction by using a compass. Draw a circle centred at B, with a radius of 5 cm. All points on this circle are the same distance from its centre. So every point on it is 5 cm from B. The correct point A can be found on this circle.

Next, draw a circle centred at C, with a radius of 5 cm. Look where the two circles meet. Their intersection gives the point A. Only parts of the two circles are needed to find A.

Join A to B and A to C using straight lines. These are the lines AB and AC. Then draw an arc centred at A. Choose the arc so that it touches B and C. You have now completed the construction.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Finding a Point Equally Far Away
activities.body: A point that is equally far from two points is equidistant from them. Each border line of the house is 5 cm long. The house needs point A, 5 cm from both B and C. Draw circles with centres B and C, each with radius 5 cm. Their intersection gives point A, which is 5 cm from both. Join A to B and C with straight lines.
keyPoints: Point A is 5 cm from both B and C.
Each circle has a radius of 5 cm.
The two circles intersect at point A.
activities.explanation: Two equal-radius circles show where the point is equally far.

activities.prompt: A circle centred at B has a radius of 5 cm.
activities.explanation: Correct! The circle centred at B has a radius of 5 cm.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the construction with its detail.
activities.explanation: The circles meet at A. Their centres are B and C, and each radius is 5 cm.

activities.prompt: Which tool can simplify the construction?
options: A compass
Trial and error only
Only one circle
A house border line
activities.explanation: Correct! The compass simplifies the construction.

activities.prompt: Finding the point with a ruler does not need trial and error.
activities.explanation: False. Finding the point with a ruler needs trial and error.

activities.prompt: A toy house has 4 border lines. Every border line is 5 cm long. What is the total length of all the border lines in cm?
activities.explanation: Total length = 5 x n. For n = 2, 3, 4, or 5, the answers are 10, 15, 20, or 25 cm.

activities.prompt: Point A is the same distance from B and C. AC is 2 cm. What is AB, in cm?
activities.explanation: A is the same distance from B and C, so AB = AC = d. For d = 2, 3, 4 or 5, the answer is 2, 3, 4 or 5 cm.

activities.prompt: Riya uses a ruler to try different points. For one point A, both AB and AC are 4 cm. What is the total length of AB and AC in cm?
activities.explanation: Total length = d + d = 2 x d. For d = 2, 3, 4, or 5, the answers are 4, 6, 8, or 10 cm.

activities.prompt: Riya uses a compass to draw a circle centred at B. She wants the circle to pass through A, and BA is 4 cm. What compass radius should she use in cm?
activities.explanation: The compass radius must equal BA. For r = 3, 4, 5, or 6, the correct radius is 3, 4, 5, or 6 cm.

activities.prompt: A circle centred at B has radius 4 cm. Point A lies on this circle. What is the length of BA in cm?
activities.explanation: Every point on a circle is the same distance from its centre. For r = 3, 4, 5, or 6, BA is 3, 4, 5, or 6 cm.

activities.prompt: A circle centred at C has radius 6 cm. Point A is where this circle meets the circle centred at B. What is the length of CA in cm?
activities.explanation: A lies on the circle centred at C, so CA is its radius. For r = 3, 4, 5, or 6, the answers are 3, 4, 5, or 6 cm.
