chapters.title: Symmetry
chapters.summary: In this chapter: seeing symmetry in patterns; lines of symmetry; reflection and making symmetrical shapes; rotational symmetry.

lessons.title: Seeing Symmetry in Patterns

activities.prompt: What might make a colourful pattern look special when you turn it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Patterns in Sight
activities.body:
You meet a flower. Look at it from many different angles. The flower looks the same from many different angles.

Now a butterfly appears, showing very attractive colours. Notice how repeated parts of a figure can follow a definite pattern. You compare each shape before deciding what matches.

Next, you see red petals in a rangoli. Turn the picture and watch those petals. They come back onto themselves after a turn. The petals return when you rotate the rangoli by 90˚ around its centre. The other parts return in the same way.

After that, you meet a pinwheel. Start with its hexagon. You can spot the repeating pattern by looking there first. Then your eyes follow the repeated parts around the pinwheel.

Finally, you look at a set of pictures. The first four pictures are symmetrical, but the last one is not. You also meet a cloud picture. It is not symmetrical. The clouds have no repetitive pattern. You now know that symmetry means parts of a figure repeat in a definite pattern.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What Is Symmetry?
activities.body: Symmetry means that parts of a figure repeat in a definite pattern. The flower looks the same from many angles. The rangoli's red petals return after a turn. Its other parts return too. A pinwheel's repeating pattern can be spotted by looking at its hexagon. The first four pictures are symmetrical, but the last one is not.
keyPoints: Symmetry means parts repeat in a definite pattern.
The rangoli's petals return after a turn.
A pinwheel's hexagon helps reveal its pattern.
activities.explanation: Look for parts that return in the same way.

activities.title: Turning a Picture
activities.body: A turn can reveal symmetry. When the rangoli turns by 90˚ around its centre, its red petals return. The other parts return in the same way. Symmetry is not present in every picture. The cloud picture is not symmetrical. Its clouds also have no repetitive pattern.
keyPoints: The rangoli's petals return after a 90˚ turn.
The other parts return in the same way.
The cloud picture is not symmetrical.
activities.explanation: A useful clue is checking which parts return after a turn.

activities.prompt: Which statement about repeated parts is correct?
options: They can follow a definite pattern.
They must follow a changing pattern.
They never form a pattern.
They can form any shape at random.
activities.explanation: Repeated parts can follow a definite pattern. This is an important part of symmetry.

activities.prompt: The red petals of the rangoli return after a turn.
activities.explanation: The red petals come back onto themselves after a turn.

activities.prompt: A tray has 4 rows of 5 marbles. How many marbles are on the tray?
activities.explanation: The repeating rows have rows × each = 20 marbles.

activities.prompt: A rangoli has 5 repeated sections, with 4 red petals in each section. How many red petals are there?
activities.explanation: The repeated sections have sections × petals = 20 red petals.

activities.prompt: A flower has 4 petals in each of 2 matching views. How many petals are seen in all the views?
activities.explanation: Each matching view shows the same petals, so petals × views = 8 petals are seen altogether.

activities.prompt: A butterfly picture has 3 matching colour spots in each of 4 repeating groups. How many colour spots are there?
activities.explanation: The repeating groups have spots × groups = 12 colour spots.

activities.prompt: The rangoli turns by 90˚ around its centre. What happens next?
options: The red petals return, and the other parts return too.
The red petals return, but the other parts stay changed.
The red petals disappear, and the other parts stay changed.
The red petals stay changed, and the other parts disappear.
activities.explanation: The petals return after a 90˚ turn. The other parts return in the same way.

activities.prompt: A pinwheel's hexagon has 4 sides, and its hexagon pattern repeats 3 times. How many hexagon sides are in the repeated pattern?
activities.explanation: Looking at the hexagon first shows sides × copies = 12 sides in the repeated pattern.

activities.prompt: There are 5 pictures. The last 2 pictures are not symmetrical (not the same on both sides). The other pictures are symmetrical. How many pictures are symmetrical?
activities.explanation: Subtract the picture that is not symmetrical: total - bad = 3 symmetrical pictures.

lessons.title: Lines of Symmetry

activities.prompt: What makes a dotted line special for a shape?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Perfect Folding Tour
activities.body:
Imagine you meet a blue triangle with a dotted line. You imagine folding along the dotted line. You lift one side and place it over the other. One half covers the other half completely.

That perfect covering tells you the fold works. Two matching halves are called mirror halves. The folding line is called a line of symmetry. Now you know what to look for during this tour.

Next, you find a square and imagine different folds. A vertical fold gives a line of symmetry in a square. A horizontal fold also gives you one. A diagonal fold gives another line of symmetry in the square.

Try the two puzzle-piece halves as you continue. These two puzzle-piece halves are not mirror halves. They fail the perfect-overlap test. So their folding line cannot be a line of symmetry.

Finally, you notice that one shape can offer several perfect folds. A figure can have more than one line of symmetry. The square guides you through this idea. Your turn is to hunt for lines that make matching halves.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What Is a Line of Symmetry?
activities.body: A line of symmetry cuts a figure into two parts that exactly overlap. The folding line is called a line of symmetry. If you fold along it, one half covers the other half completely. These matching halves are called mirror halves. A square has lines of symmetry from vertical, horizontal and diagonal folds. A figure can have more than one line of symmetry.
keyPoints: The two parts exactly overlap.
The folding line is called a line of symmetry.
Matching halves are called mirror halves.
activities.explanation: Lines of symmetry help matching halves fit together perfectly.

activities.prompt: A child folds each of 4 square papers once. Each fold line is called a line of symmetry. How many lines of symmetry are there in all?

activities.prompt: Put these sentences in order to describe a line of symmetry.

The folding line is called a line of symmetry.

lessons.title: Reflection and Making Symmetrical Shapes

activities.prompt: What might appear when you fold a shape and open it again?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Mirror Line
activities.body:
Imagine a square with labelled corners A, B, C and D. You wonder how its mirror image would look. A vertical line can act as its line of symmetry. Reflection sends one side of that line to the other.

When you reflect across the vertical line, B and C move to the left side. The reflected points occupy the earlier positions of A and D. Also, A moves to B's position, and D moves to C's position.

Picture paper with a line of symmetry down the middle. A few drops of ink or paint go onto one half. You fold the paper and press the halves together. The two halves overlap completely. You open the paper and see matching marks on both halves.

You can use folding and cutting to make symmetrical shapes. Try cutting folded paper so the opened sheet has matching halves. If your design has a line of symmetry, it has reflection symmetry.

Punch holes through folded paper. When you open it, the holes form a symmetrical pattern. Each hole matches another hole across the fold.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Fold and Reflect
activities.body: When you fold a figure along its line of symmetry, both parts overlap completely. Reflection sends one side to the other side of the line. It sends the other part back to the first side. Square corners are A, B, C and D. A figure with a line of symmetry has reflection symmetry. Folding and cutting can make symmetrical shapes. Punching holes in folded paper creates symmetrical patterns.
keyPoints: Both parts overlap completely after folding.
Reflection moves one side to the other.
The square's corners are A, B, C and D.
Cutting folded paper can make symmetrical shapes.
Punching folded paper can create symmetrical patterns.
activities.explanation: Folding and reflection help you make and recognise symmetrical shapes.

activities.prompt: Which happens when a figure folds along its line of symmetry?
options: The parts do not touch.
The parts overlap completely.
The parts overlap only partly.
The parts move to separate corners.
activities.explanation: A fold along the line of symmetry makes both parts overlap completely.

activities.prompt: Reflection leaves both sides of a line of symmetry in place.
activities.explanation: Reflection moves one side to the other side of the line.

The folded halves are pressed together.
activities.explanation: The drops come first. Then the folded halves are pressed and opened.

activities.prompt: A drawing has 5 marked points on one side of a line of symmetry. A reflection is a mirror copy across the line. How many matching points are on the other side after the reflection?
activities.explanation: A reflection gives one matching point for each marked point.

activities.prompt: A square has sides of 8 cm. A line of symmetry goes straight up and down. It cuts the square into two equal halves. How wide is each half, in cm?
activities.explanation: The two overlapping halves each have half the side length of the square.

activities.prompt: A square has side 8 cm. A vertical reflection pairs its two vertical sides. What is their total length, in cm?
activities.explanation: Each vertical side is s cm long, so their total length is 2 × s cm.

activities.prompt: A drawing has 4 points on one side of a line of symmetry. Its reflection, a mirror copy, is added. How many points are there in total?
activities.explanation: The drawing has n original points. It also has n matching reflected points.

activities.prompt: There are 6 drops of ink on one half of a folded paper. After the halves are pressed together and opened, how many matching ink marks are there?
activities.explanation: Each drop leaves one matching mark on the other half.

activities.prompt: A child folds a paper once. Then 5 shapes are cut through the folded paper. The paper is opened. How many matching shapes are there in all?
activities.explanation: Cutting through the folded paper makes one matching shape on each half.

lessons.title: Rotational Symmetry

activities.prompt: How can a shape look unchanged without folding perfectly onto itself?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Turning the Windmill
activities.body:
You meet a paper windmill. It looks symmetrical, yet it has no line of symmetry. Try folding its two halves. They do not exactly overlap, so the fold test fails.

Turn the windmill through 90° about its centre. It looks exactly the same. This shows that the windmill has rotational symmetry.

Rotational symmetry always has a fixed point about which the object turns. This fixed point is called the centre of rotation. Try a turn smaller than 90°. The windmill does not look the same.

An angle of symmetry makes a figure look exactly the same after rotation. The windmill has symmetry angles of 90° and 180°. It also has symmetry angles of 270° and 360°. A 360° angle is always an angle of symmetry.

A square gives another example. It overlaps with itself after a 90° rotation. Compare folding with turning. The windmill passes the turning test, but not the folding test.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What is rotational symmetry?
activities.body: Rotational symmetry means an object looks exactly the same after it turns about a fixed point. This fixed point is called the centre of rotation. The paper windmill has rotational symmetry because a 90° rotation about its centre makes it look exactly the same. Its symmetry angles are 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. It has no line of symmetry.
keyPoints: Rotational symmetry uses a fixed point.
The fixed point is the centre of rotation.
The windmill has symmetry angles of 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you recognise rotational symmetry.

tasks.then: A turn of 120 degrees brings it back into a matching position.

tasks.say: Keep turning until it matches again.
tasks.then: It matches at 120 and 240 degrees, and again at 360.

activities.takeaway: The order of rotation counts how many times a shape matches itself in one full turn.
activities.explanation: The order of rotation counts how many times a shape matches itself in one full turn.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the paper windmill is true?
options: It looks the same after a 90° rotation.
It has no centre of rotation.
Its two halves overlap when folded.
It looks the same after any turn less than 90°.
activities.explanation: A 90° rotation about its centre makes the windmill look exactly the same.

activities.prompt: Match each angle with the correct statement.

activities.explanation: These four angles are symmetry angles of the windmill.

activities.prompt: What does the windmill do after a turn of less than 90°?
options: It does not look the same.

It becomes a square.
activities.explanation: The windmill does not look the same after a turn of less than 90°.

activities.prompt: A windmill looks exactly the same after a 180° turn about its centre. How many degrees is that angle of symmetry?
activities.explanation: The angle of symmetry is 180°, so the answer is 180.

activities.prompt: A windmill looks the same after each 90° turn. It turns 5 times. How many degrees does it turn in all?
activities.explanation: The total turn is 5 x 90 = 450 degrees.

activities.explanation: The correct order is 90°, 180°, 270°, then 360°.

activities.prompt: A windmill is turned through 180°, 180°, 270°, and 90°. Each listed turn is an angle of symmetry. What is the total of the four turns in degrees?
activities.explanation: The total angle is 180+180+270+90=720 degrees.

activities.prompt: A paper spinner has 1 equal steps in one full turn. It looks the same after all 1 steps. What is the angle of the full turn in degrees?
activities.explanation: (360/1)*1=360 degrees. A 360° angle is always an angle of symmetry.

activities.prompt: A square with side 8 cm overlaps itself after a 90° turn. What is its perimeter after the turn in cm?
activities.explanation: The square overlaps itself, so its perimeter remains 8*4=32 cm.

lessons.title: Rotational Symmetry with Radial Arms

activities.prompt: What could you discover by turning a radial-arm cutout?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Rotating Radial-Arm Figures
activities.body:
You begin with a radial-arm figure on two pieces of paper. Cut it out carefully.

You explore the four-arm figure first. The adjacent central dotted lines are 90° apart. Then try changing it so it has only two symmetry angles.

You rotate your cutout. This helps you check whether the figure has rotational symmetry. Watch the arms and compare their positions.

You now meet an unequal three-arm figure. It has no rotational symmetry. To make a three-arm design overlap, angle A must overlap angle B.

You next explore a symmetrical three-arm design. All three angles must be equal. The angle between adjacent arms is 120°. For five arms, the symmetry angles are 72°, 144°, 216°, 288° and 360°. For six arms, they are 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300° and 360°. Each angle is a multiple of the smallest angle.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Checking Rotational Symmetry
activities.body: Rotating a cutout helps us check a figure for rotational symmetry. In the four-arm figure, adjacent central dotted lines are 90° apart. The symmetrical three-arm design has 120° between adjacent arms. The unequal three-arm figure has no rotational symmetry. Five-arm angles are 72°, 144°, 216°, 288° and 360°. Six-arm angles are 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300° and 360°. Symmetry angles are multiples of the smallest angle.
keyPoints: A rotating cutout helps check rotational symmetry.
Adjacent arms have equal angles in a symmetrical design.
Symmetry angles are multiples of the smallest angle.
activities.explanation: Rotating the cutout helps us check whether the figure has rotational symmetry.

tasks.say: Turn it until it looks the same.
tasks.then: A turn of 120 degrees brings it back into a matching position.

tasks.say: Keep turning until it matches again.
tasks.then: It matches at 120 and 240 degrees, and again at 360.

activities.takeaway: The order of rotation counts how many times a shape matches itself in one full turn.
activities.explanation: The order of rotation counts how many times a shape matches itself in one full turn.

activities.prompt: Match each design with the angle between its adjacent parts.
activities.explanation: Each pair uses an angle stated for that design.

activities.explanation: To overlap, angle B must equal angle A. Thus, the required value is a degrees.

activities.explanation: A full turn is 360°. Dividing 360 by arms gives 120°, 90°, 72°, or 60° for 3, 4, 5, or 6 arms.

lessons.title: Symmetry of Circles and the Whole Chapter

activities.prompt: What makes a circle seem unchanged, even when it spins?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Circle Symmetry Tour
activities.body:
Imagine a circle waiting quietly. You turn it, and it looks exactly the same. Would you call this symmetry?

You can turn it through any angle, and it still matches itself. A circle therefore coincides with itself after any rotation. Every diameter is also a line of symmetry for the circle.

Now you meet fans, flowers and wheels. These objects show rotational symmetry. Some figures have several lines of symmetry. Others may have several angles of symmetry.

An angle of symmetry lies strictly between 0° and 360°. If a figure has such an angle, it has rotational symmetry. The point where you turn it is called the centre of rotation.

You see that some figures have a line of symmetry but no angle of symmetry. Other figures have angles of symmetry but no lines of symmetry. Then you find shapes with both lines and angles of symmetry. So, what makes a figure seem unchanged? You compare its lines, angles and centre of rotation.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Circles and Symmetry
activities.body: An angle of symmetry shows rotational symmetry. A circle matches itself after any rotation. Its centre is the point of rotation. Every diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry. An angle of symmetry is strictly between 0° and 360°. A figure can have several lines, several angles, or both kinds of symmetry.
keyPoints: A circle matches itself after any rotation.
Every diameter is a line of symmetry.
Symmetry can involve lines, angles, or both.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you recognise different kinds of symmetry.

activities.title: Different Kinds of Symmetry
activities.body: Different figures show different kinds of symmetry. Some have a line of symmetry but no angle of symmetry. Others have angles of symmetry but no lines. Some have both. Fans, flowers and wheels show rotational symmetry. A circle has special strength: it matches itself after any rotation, and every diameter is a line of symmetry.
keyPoints: Some figures have lines but no angles.
Others have angles but no lines.
Some figures have both kinds.
activities.explanation: A figure can show different kinds of symmetry.

activities.title: What Happens After Rotation?
activities.prompt: What happens to a circle after a rotation through any angle?
options: It coincides with itself.
It becomes a straight line.
It becomes a different circle.
It loses all symmetry.
activities.explanation: A circle coincides with itself after any rotation. This shows rotational symmetry.

activities.title: A Diameter and Symmetry
activities.prompt: Every diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry.
activities.explanation: Every diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry.

activities.title: Match the Meanings

activities.explanation: Each pair matches the meaning given in this chapter.

activities.prompt: A round plate turns 60 degrees around its centre. It looks the same after the turn. It turns 2 times. How many degrees does it turn in all?
activities.explanation: A circle looks the same after any rotation. Total degrees = 60 × 2 = 120°.

activities.prompt: A toy fan turns 60 degrees around its centre. It looks the same after the turn. Write 1 if it has rotational symmetry. Write 0 if it does not.
activities.explanation: A fan looks the same after the turn. So it has rotational symmetry. The answer is 1.

activities.prompt: A circle has 4 marked diameters (lines through the centre). Each one is a line of symmetry. How many marked lines of symmetry does the circle have?
activities.explanation: Every diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry. So the number of marked lines of symmetry is 4.

activities.prompt: A design has 5 different lines of symmetry. It has 3 different angles of symmetry. How many symmetry features are there in all?
activities.explanation: The design has several lines of symmetry and several angles of symmetry. Altogether, the number is 5 + 3 = 8.

activities.prompt: An angle of symmetry is chosen as 360° minus 4°. What is the angle of symmetry in degrees?
activities.explanation: An angle of symmetry lies strictly between 0° and 360°. Thus, 360° − 4° gives the valid angle 356°.

activities.title: Order the Rotation Steps
activities.prompt: Put these steps for rotating a circle in order.
items: Choose an angle strictly between 0° and 360°.
Rotate the circle through the chosen angle.
activities.explanation: A circle matches itself after any rotation. The chosen angle must lie strictly between 0° and 360°.

activities.prompt: A figure looks unchanged after a rotation of 15° about its centre. How many equal turns of 15° fit in one full turn?
activities.explanation: Having an angle of symmetry means that the figure has rotational symmetry. The number of equal turns is 360 ÷ 15 = 24.

lessons.title: Integers and the Building of Fun

activities.prompt: How can a lift help you discover positive and negative numbers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Lift and the Number Ray
activities.body:
Welcome aboard. You begin beside a number ray that starts at zero. Zero comes before one and means nothing. You follow the ray to the right, and it continues for ever.

You enter the lift. It can move up or down between floors. Press the plus button twice, and you rise by two floors. Going down two floors is written as −2.

Now you explore the floors. The Food Court sits on Floor +1. The Toy Store lies on Floor −1. The plus sign shows a positive number, while the minus sign shows a negative number.

You meet zero again. It is neither positive nor negative. You stand at zero and remember that it means nothing.

Before you leave, you meet ten digits. Together, they can write numbers of any size in the Indian number system. Your journey ends, but the number ray keeps going right for ever.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Zero, signs, and moving floors
activities.body: Zero comes before 1 and means nothing. The number ray begins at 0 and continues right for ever. Ten digits can write numbers of any size in the Indian number system. Plus signs mark positive numbers, and minus signs mark negative numbers. Zero is neither positive nor negative. A lift moves up and down between floors. Going down two floors is written as – 2.
keyPoints: 0 represents nothing and comes before 1.
Positive numbers have plus signs; negative numbers have minus signs.
The lift moves between floors; down two floors is – 2.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you read signs and move between floors.

up two floors
nothing

activities.explanation: The Food Court is on Floor +1. Going down two floors reaches the Toy Store on Floor –1.

The lift moves up two floors

lessons.title: Moving, Comparing and Finding Change

activities.prompt: Ready to discover what changes when a lift moves?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Lift Journey
activities.body:
You stand at the starting floor beside a lift. Its buttons invite you to explore movement. The starting floor plus the movement gives the target floor.

From Floor + 1, move by two floors. Moving from Floor + 1 by two floors reaches Floor + 3. Combining button presses is a form of addition. You can check the target by finding the movement needed.

Now try the reverse. The inverse of + 3 is – 3. Pressing the inverse of a floor number takes the lift back to zero. A positive movement and its inverse add to zero.

Compare nearby floors as you travel. Floor + 3 is lower than Floor + 4. Floor – 4 is lower than Floor – 3. Every negative number is less than zero. Every positive number is greater than zero.

Perhaps two quantities differ. Subtraction can mean making two unequal quantities equal. Find the starting floor, then find the target. The movement needed is the target floor minus the starting floor.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Lift Movements Work
activities.body: A lift’s starting floor and movement give its target floor. Moving up by three floors from Floor + 1 reaches Floor + 3. Combining button presses is addition. An inverse movement undoes another movement. The inverse of + 3 is – 3. A positive movement and its inverse make zero. You can compare floors and find the needed movement.
keyPoints: Add the movement to the starting floor.
The inverse of + 3 is – 3.
A movement and its inverse make zero.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you move, compare and undo lift movements.

tasks.then: You cross zero and land on -4.

activities.explanation: The inverse of + 3 is – 3. These movements make zero together.

activities.title: Match Each Idea
activities.prompt: Match each left-hand idea with its correct meaning.
activities.explanation: Inverse movements undo each other, and the facts compare floors and numbers.

activities.prompt: A lift starts at Floor 5 and must reach Floor 8. What upward movement is needed, in floors?
activities.explanation: Subtract the starting floor number from the target floor number: target - start. For example, 7 - 2 = 5 floors.

activities.prompt: A lift is at Floor 7 + 1. It moves up 2 floors. What floor number does it reach?
activities.explanation: Add the starting floor number and the upward movement: f + 1 + 2. The lift reaches Floor 7 + 3.

activities.prompt: A lift goes up 6 floors. Then it goes up 3 more floors. How many floors does it go up in all?
activities.explanation: Combining the two button presses is addition: a + b. The total upward movement is 9 floors.

activities.prompt: A lift is at Floor 2 + 3. The down button moves it down 3 floors. What floor number does it reach?
activities.explanation: The inverse of + 3 is - 3, so add 3 and then subtract 3: f + 3 - 3. The lift reaches Floor 2.

activities.title: Plan a Lift Journey
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the right order. Use them to plan a lift trip.
items: Find the target floor (where you want to go)
Subtract the starting floor from the target floor
activities.explanation: The needed movement is the target floor minus the starting floor. Add the movement to the starting floor to reach the target.

activities.prompt: One lift is 3 floors above Floor 0, and another is 2 floors below Floor 0. How many floors apart are their floor numbers?
activities.explanation: The floor numbers are a and 0 - b. Their distance is a - (0 - b), which is a + b floors.

activities.prompt: Which floor number is lower, Floor 7 + 3 or Floor 7 - 4?
activities.explanation: A floor below Floor 7 is lower than one above Floor 7. Therefore, Floor 7 - 4 is lower.

lessons.title: Number Lines and Large Integers

activities.prompt: How can a tiny minus sign help you travel across a huge number line?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Large Numbers
activities.body:
You begin your tour at zero. Negative numbers lie to the left of zero. Moving right is positive movement.

Smaller numbers stay left of larger numbers. Start at 5 and move four steps to 9. You have added 4. Turn back from 9 to 3. That journey moves – 6 steps. From 3 to – 2, you move – 5 steps.

Now imagine subtracting a negative number. This works like adding the corresponding positive number. The operation becomes addition of the matching positive number.

Next, compare + 2000 and – 200. Their difference is + 2200. You find it by adding the corresponding positive number, 200.

Finally, remember that subtraction can always become addition. Use the inverse of the number being subtracted. Positive numbers usually leave out the plus sign. Your number-line tour now has a simple rule.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Reading and Moving on a Number Line
activities.body: Number lines help you see how numbers sit and move. Negative numbers lie to the left of zero. Smaller numbers lie to the left of larger numbers. Moving right shows a positive direction. Moving from 5 to 9 adds 4, while moving from 9 to 3 moves – 6 steps. Subtracting a negative number acts like adding its positive counterpart. You can also change subtraction into addition by using an inverse.
keyPoints: Negative numbers lie to the left of zero.
Moving right shows the positive direction.
Subtracting a negative number works like adding a positive number.
activities.explanation: Number lines make larger numbers and negative movements easier to understand.

tasks.then: You cross zero and land on -4.

activities.takeaway: Adding a negative moves left, adding a positive moves right.
activities.explanation: Adding a negative moves left, adding a positive moves right.

activities.title: Where Negative Numbers Lie
activities.prompt: On a number line, where do negative numbers lie?
options: To the left of zero
To the right of zero
Above zero
Below zero
activities.explanation: Negative numbers lie to the left of zero.

activities.title: Writing Positive Numbers
activities.prompt: The plus sign is usually left out when writing positive numbers.
activities.explanation: Yes. Positive numbers are usually written without a plus sign.

activities.title: Finding a Difference
activities.prompt: The difference between + 2000 and – 200 is + ______.
activities.explanation: The difference between + 2000 and – 200 is + 2200.

activities.title: Match Each Movement
activities.prompt: Match each movement with the correct change.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows the change in direction and size.

activities.title: Moving Right
activities.prompt: Moving to the right means moving in the negative direction.
activities.explanation: Moving to the right means moving in the positive direction.

activities.title: Moving Across Zero
activities.prompt: What movement takes you from 3 to – 2?
options: – 5 steps
+ 5 steps
– 2 steps
+ 2 steps
activities.explanation: Moving from 3 to – 2 means moving – 5 steps.

activities.title: Order Numbers on a Number Line
activities.prompt: Put these numbers in order from left to right on a number line.
activities.explanation: Negative numbers come before positive numbers. Smaller numbers come first.

lessons.title: The Token Model

activities.prompt: What happens when positive and negative tokens meet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Token Model
activities.body:
You begin on Floor 0. The lift attendant is there with an empty pocket. This is your starting point.

You see green positive tokens and red negative tokens. You press the plus button, and you take a positive token. You press the minus button, and you take a negative token.

Now you meet five positive tokens and three negative tokens together. Their value is + 2. You discover that one positive token and one negative token cancel each other. Together, they make a zero pair.

You remove all zero pairs from the five positive and three negative tokens. Two positive tokens remain. The token model shows that subtraction can work through tokens too.

Try adding + 5 and – 8. Your sum is – 3. Then find the difference between – 7 and – 5. The difference is – 2. You now see how tokens can represent positive and negative values.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Positive, Negative and Zero Pairs
activities.body: The lift attendant uses two kinds of tokens. Green tokens are positive. Red tokens are negative. Pressing the plus button means taking a positive token. Pressing the minus button means taking a negative token. A positive token and a negative token cancel each other. Together, they make a zero pair. Removing zero pairs shows the final value.
keyPoints: Green tokens are positive.
Red tokens are negative.
A positive and negative token make a zero pair.
activities.explanation: This model shows how positive and negative tokens work together.

activities.prompt: Which token is positive?
options: The green token
The red token
The empty pocket
activities.explanation: Green tokens are positive, while red tokens are negative.

activities.prompt: A lift attendant starts with an empty pocket. The attendant presses the plus button 2 times. What is the value in token units?
activities.explanation: Each press of the plus button adds one positive token. So 2 positive tokens have a value of 2 token units.

activities.prompt: The lift worker presses the plus button 4 times. The lift worker presses the minus button 1 time. What is the total pocket value, in token units?
activities.explanation: The positive tokens add 4. The negative tokens subtract 1. So the total is 4 - 1 token units.

activities.prompt: The pocket has 6 positive tokens and 5 negative tokens. After removing all zero pairs, how many positive tokens remain?
activities.explanation: Each negative token cancels one positive token. After removing the zero pairs, 6 - 5 positive tokens remain.

activities.prompt: Match each token situation to its result.
pairs: Five positive and three negative tokens
One positive token and one negative token
Five positive and three negative tokens, with zero pairs removed
activities.explanation: A zero pair cancels, so only two positive tokens remain.

activities.prompt: Put the token steps in order.
items: Five positive and three negative tokens
activities.explanation: Removing zero pairs leaves two positive tokens and a value of + 2.

activities.prompt: What is the sum of + 5 and – 8?
activities.explanation: The sum of + 5 and – 8 is – 3.

activities.prompt: A marble tray has 10 marbles. The lift attendant uses 3 negative tokens to take marbles away, one marble for each token. How many marbles remain?
activities.explanation: Taking away 3 marbles from 10 marbles leaves 10 - 3 marbles.

lessons.title: Integers in Banking, Heights and Temperature

activities.prompt: How can one number show money, height and temperature all at once?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Banking, Heights and Temperature
activities.body:
You begin at the bank and open your passbook. A credit appears when money is added. A debit appears when money is taken out.

Next, you imagine that some banks allow an account balance to become negative temporarily. A bank may charge interest or a fee when the balance is negative. It is generally better to try to keep a positive bank balance.

Now you change your viewpoint. Credits can be treated as positive numbers, while debits can be treated as negative numbers.

After that, you explore the idea of sea level. The height at sea level is 0 metres. Heights above sea level are represented by positive numbers. Heights below sea level are represented by negative numbers.

Finally, you visit a thermometer. Celsius is the unit used for measuring temperature. You see that 0°C indicates the freezing point of water.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Understanding positive and negative numbers
activities.body: In a bank passbook, a credit means money added. A debit means money taken out. Credits can be positive, while debits can be negative. Some banks let balances become negative, and may then charge interest or a fee. For heights, sea level is 0 metres, above it is positive, and below it is negative. Temperature is measured in Celsius. At 0°C, water is at its freezing point.
keyPoints: Credits can be positive, and debits can be negative.
Heights above sea level are positive, and heights below it are negative.
Celsius is the unit used for measuring temperature.
activities.explanation: These signs help you read banking, heights and temperature.

tasks.then: You cross zero and land on -4.
A number and its opposite make zero.

activities.takeaway: Adding a negative moves left, adding a positive moves right.
activities.explanation: Adding a negative moves left, adding a positive moves right.

activities.title: What does a credit show?
activities.prompt: A credit in a bank passbook shows that money has been:
options: taken out
added
measured
charged
activities.explanation: A credit is shown when money is added to a bank account.

activities.title: Debits and money
activities.prompt: A bank passbook shows a debit when money is taken out.
activities.explanation: A debit shows money leaving the bank account.

activities.prompt: A bank passbook shows a credit of 100 rupees. What is the signed credit amount in rupees?
activities.explanation: A credit is positive, so the signed amount is 100 rupees.

activities.prompt: An account has 750 rupees and receives a credit of 500 rupees. What is the new balance in rupees?
activities.explanation: Adding the credit gives 750+500 rupees.

activities.prompt: An account has 1500 rupees and a debit of 100 rupees is made. What is the new balance in rupees?
activities.explanation: Subtracting the debit gives 1500-100 rupees.

activities.prompt: An account has a credit of 700 rupees and a debit of 200 rupees. The credit is larger than the debit. What is the signed balance in rupees that the customer should try to keep?
activities.explanation: The signed balance is 700-200 rupees. It is positive, so it is better to try to keep it.

activities.title: Order the heights
activities.prompt: Put these heights in order from lowest to highest.
activities.explanation: Below sea level is negative, sea level is 0 metres, and above sea level is positive.

activities.prompt: Place A is 30 metres below sea level, where sea level is 0 metres. Place B is 60 metres above sea level. What is the difference between their heights in metres?
activities.explanation: Place A has height -30 metres. Subtracting its height from Place B's height gives 60-(-30)=60+30 metres.

lessons.title: Integer Grids and a Pinch of History

activities.prompt: Could a grid hide a secret about numbers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Grid's Number Journey
activities.body:
You meet a grid with two rows and two columns. The sum of the two rows and two columns is called the border sum. The top and bottom rows have equal border sums. The left and right columns do too.

You choose a number in the number-grid game. Its row and column are struck out. The circled numbers in the example add to – 1.

Your journey moves to Asia many centuries ago. General integers were first conceived and used there. The earliest known uses of negative numbers occurred in accounting. You wonder about signs.

You visit the Nine Chapters on Mathematical Art. It was completed by the first or second century CE. Kautilya wrote about credit and debit around 300 BCE. The Bakśhālī manuscript used a special sign after a negative number around 300 CE. Finally, Brahmagupta gave equal treatment to positive numbers, negative numbers and zero in 628 CE. His equal treatment of these numbers formed what is now called a ring. You carry this history back to your grid.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What are integer grids?
activities.body: Integer grids are a number game with a border sum. This sum comes from the two rows and two columns. The top and bottom rows share a border sum. The left and right columns share one too. When you choose a number, its row and column are struck out. The history of integers includes uses of negative numbers in accounting. Brahmagupta treated positive numbers, negative numbers and zero equally.
keyPoints: A border sum uses two rows and two columns.
Opposite rows and columns share border sums.
Choosing a number strikes out its row and column.
activities.explanation: You will explore grid rules and the history of integers.

activities.prompt: The border sum uses the top row and the bottom row. It also uses the left and right columns.
activities.explanation: Yes. The border sum uses both rows and both columns.

activities.prompt: In the number grid game, when you pick a number, you cross out its ______ and column.
activities.hint: It is one part of the grid.
activities.explanation: You pick a number. You cross out its whole row and column.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the grid is true?
options: The border sum uses only the top row.
The top and bottom rows have the same border sum.
The left and right columns have different border sums.
activities.explanation: The top and bottom rows always have the same border sum.

activities.prompt: A 2 by 2 laddoo grid has rows (6, 5) and (5, 6). Add the sums of the two rows and two columns. What is the border sum in laddoos?
activities.explanation: Each row and each column sums to a+b laddoos. Therefore, the border sum is 4*(a+b) = 4*(2+3) = 20 laddoos.

activities.prompt: Three entries in a rupee grid, -4, 2, and -1, are circled. The circled numbers must add to -1. What value must -1 have in rupees?
activities.explanation: Since a+b+c must equal -1, c must be -1-(a+b). For example, -1-(-4+2) = 1 rupee.

activities.prompt: Which sentence best tells what Brahmagupta did for integers?
options: He finished the Nine Chapters on Mathematical Art.
He wrote about credit and debit around 300 BCE.
He treated positive numbers, negative numbers and zero the same in 628 CE.
He used a special sign after a negative number around 300 CE.
activities.explanation: Brahmagupta treated all these numbers the same. This idea is now called a ring.

activities.prompt: Negative numbers were first used in Asia long ago. People used them in accounts. Kautilya wrote about credit and debit around 300 BCE. How many years before 1 CE was that?
activities.explanation: Kautilya wrote around 300 BCE, so the number of years before 1 CE is k = 300 years.
